sources.title: Dalton Caldwell: Build startups that create more wealth than they capture
sources.originalTitle: The Startup Ideas that Create the Most Wealth
sources.summary: Dalton and PB of Standard Capital explain how wealth is created (positive-sum exchange, marketplaces, better decisions) and why founders should know exactly where their startup creates it. Dalton's advice: make customers far better off than you, and capture only a slice of the value you create.

principles.text: Know exactly how your startup creates wealth for users and customers; the more, the better.
principles.quote: you should understand how your startup is creating wealth. And the more wealth you create for your users and your customers, the better.

principles.text: Create more value than you capture, and be clear on where the wealth is created.
principles.quote: our advice is to create more value than you capture and have a really good idea on where the wealth is being created by your startup.

principles.text: Test for wealth creation by comparing the value customers get against what the startup itself gets.
principles.quote: I like to think about how much value the customers of a startup are getting versus the startup itself to know if they're making wealth.

principles.text: Being slightly cheaper than a competitor is not value creation; be far better than the alternatives.
principles.quote: it's creating value not necessarily because you're the lowest cost solution versus a competitor. It's that you're so much better than other options.

principles.text: Real wealth creation is positive-sum: you add value without cheating or stealing from anyone.
principles.quote: you didn't cheat anyone, you didn't steal, you you put labor into an action and it created more value than what the labor was worth.

principles.text: Sort ideas by whether they are positive-sum and create wealth; the real question is which bucket a startup falls in.
principles.quote: We just have a different criteria about who's in the bucket of positive sum things that create wealth and who's not.

sources.title: Founders Should Avoid Bad Investors: how to spot them and what good ones do
sources.originalTitle: Founders Should Avoid Bad Investors
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell and PB (Standard Capital) explain what separates good from bad angel investors. Bad ones fear loss, slow-walk diligence, try to control founders and often have no real budget; good ones move fast, diversify and accept most bets go to zero. Includes concrete screening questions for founders.

principles.text: Judge an investor by their actual track record: ask how many investments they made last year, check sizes, and call those founders.
principles.quote: how many other investments have you made in the past year, how big were the checks, and what were they? And then you could contact you know, you could like look if it's on the website that's fine, but you could contact those people

principles.text: Many bad investors have no money or a tiny budget; they meet hundreds of founders to make one investment or try to act as middlemen.
principles.quote: They're just trying to insert themselves as a middleman between someone with money and a startup.

principles.text: Slow fundraising processes are a bad sign and cause adverse selection: only founders with no alternatives tolerate slow investors.
principles.quote: the slowest investors have the worst returns.

principles.text: Sophisticated investors keep their process light; elaborate process is a sign of inexperience.
principles.quote: The sign of a good investor is often that their process is great. Um because it means they're sophisticated.

principles.text: Early-stage investing rewards diversification: spread across many checks rather than one big bet, since outcomes are inherently unpredictable.
principles.quote: you want to split up the number of checks you you write. It's like you get to roll the dice.

principles.text: Good investors write the check, then mentally kiss the money goodbye; panic, clawing money back or micromanaging founders hurts the company.
principles.quote: you write the check and then step two is you kiss the money goodbye.

sources.title: Founder info hazards: feeds, LLM sycophancy and staying grounded
sources.originalTitle: What Are Founder Info Hazards?
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell and PB discuss how feeds and LLMs can distort a founder's thinking, drawing on Dalton's FriendFeed experience creating the like button. The fix is limits, gaps away from screens, and grounding in real people and real customers who say no to your product.

principles.text: Cap time on feeds; most value comes early and harm accumulates with doom scrolling.
principles.quote: I feel like I get the most value in the first 10 minutes. But then like the most harm is done

principles.text: Feeds are sand that crowds out substance; you must cut yourself off because they have no end.
principles.quote: if you take too much, there's there's no room for anything of substance. And so, a lot of times, the hardest thing is just cutting yourself off

principles.text: Don't use LLMs or social platforms as a mirror to judge who you are.
principles.quote: not ever holding up these technologies is a mirror of yourself.

principles.text: Be wary of LLMs validating big life decisions or grand claims, since they affirm rather than push back.
principles.quote: be especially um wary of the LLM validating big life decisions or [clears throat] fantastical claims not backed in reality about your abilities.

principles.text: Take regular gaps away from these tools to come up for air; a good test is whether you can disconnect.
principles.quote: Having gaps where you essentially come up for air, I think is is pretty essential

principles.text: Selling is grounding: asking for money exposes whether everyone really wants your product.
principles.quote: actually trying to sell products is is a form of grounding. Because when you ask people for money, they say no.

sources.title: After Your Series A: Hiring Pace, Burn Discipline and Setting 12-Month Goals (Standard Capital)
sources.originalTitle: You Just Raised Series A. Now what?
sources.summary: Dalton and PB of Standard Capital share what founders should do right after a Series A. Hire gradually into roles you understand, set a hard 12-month goal, spend only into proven channels and bank the rest, and treat the round as a starting line, not a finish line.

principles.text: Understand every level of your startup well enough to do the work yourself before you hire for it.
principles.quote: our advice to founders is understand every level of your startup and make sure you can do every level of work at a startup.

principles.text: Ease hires in gradually; flooding a small team with new people can wreck culture, but under-hiring is also a mistake.
principles.quote: you could totally wreck your culture if you had five people and you hire 20.

principles.text: After the A, set a concrete 12-month goal (e.g. ~$2M to $10M ARR) and use channels that scale beyond seed-stage tactics.
principles.quote: setting that 12-month goal is key.

principles.text: Spend aggressively only into a channel that demonstrably pays back; otherwise bank the money rather than burn it.
principles.quote: if you have a very effective channel for growth and you could spend into it, then you want to spend into it and and it'll pay back so you could be aggressive.

principles.text: Don't burn all your cash to look like growth; start burning only once you know it works, and avoid relying on a greater fool.
principles.quote: only start burning once you really know it works.

principles.text: A Series A is a starting line, not a finish line; the game keeps getting harder as you succeed.
principles.quote: congratulations, you won the prize. Your your award is more work.

sources.title: Dalton Caldwell on revenue multiples: why comps and market size decide your startup's valuation
sources.originalTitle: How Investors Actually Value Companies
sources.summary: Dalton and Paul of Standard Capital explain why public-market revenue multiples set the ceiling for startup valuations. Key warning: AI-enabled service companies get valued like the legacy service firms they disrupt unless founders prove a technology-sized, growing market.

principles.text: Public-market multiples for your category flow downstream into what startups in that category can raise at.
principles.quote: a lot of SaaS companies are trading horribly. Like their their revenue multiples are very low and it's bad and that downwind effect totally hurts startups that are doing SaaS because those are the the comparables that they are valued against, right?

principles.text: Know your comps before you pitch. Research what comparable companies are worth and have a story for why you will be worth far more.
principles.quote: I do think that's an exercise every should do is do the research on what the comparables are and how they are valued and then have a really good story on why you're going to be worth way more than those if the comparables aren't great.

principles.text: AI-enabled service startups risk being valued like the low-multiple service firms they replace; you must prove you deserve tech multiples.
principles.quote: you need to have proof points and a story on why you should be valued as a technology company with technology company multiples, and not as the service company you're disrupting.

principles.text: Legacy service companies trade at roughly 1x to 2x revenue, so a service-like startup can be worth very little even with real revenue.
principles.quote: So, a 2x revenue multiple on a million dollars a year is the company's worth $2 million.

principles.text: High multiples go to businesses that can grow into an unbounded market, not a fixed-size one.
principles.quote: It makes sense that SpaceX would trade at a high multiple versus it being this like fixed finite thing where there's no way it can grow, so it's valued like one or two X.

principles.text: Valuation reflects expected future cash flows, which is why a company can look overvalued for a long time while the market prices in future potential.
principles.quote: the market can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent.

sources.title: Will AI kill all startups? Turkey startups, model bets, and moats that survive
sources.originalTitle: Will AI Kill All Startups?
sources.summary: Dalton and PB from Standard Capital discuss which startups the AI labs will run over. Dalton's points: don't build workarounds for today's model flaws, hard-to-build software is no longer a moat, and the internet era shows who adapts and who gets crushed.

principles.text: Building around today's model weaknesses is an implicit bet that models won't improve, which is a losing bet.
principles.quote: some startups are implicitly making a bet that the models won't get smarter.

principles.text: Middleware that patches model deficiencies is a 'turkey startup': the next model release can wipe it out.
principles.quote: if you build all this like bread middleware to make the models work in certain use cases because they're deficient, that is the definition of a turkey startup because there's going to be a new model that drops and it's game over.

principles.text: Building on a platform's weakness is effectively shorting that platform, and you lose when it improves.
principles.quote: making a short bet on Google.

principles.text: If your moat is that the product is hard to build, expect trouble as AI makes software cheap to create.
principles.quote: So, it seems like pure software businesses where the moat is that it's hard to build are going to have a bad time.

principles.text: Incumbents facing a platform shift must adapt fast; the internet crushed slow reactors while adapters survived.
principles.quote: think about all the companies that had to react to the internet coming out.

principles.text: Energy and compute abundance expand what's possible, so the opportunity pie grows bigger for builders.
principles.quote: as energy becomes more abundant and compute becomes more abundant, the scale of what you can do easily gets bigger and bigger.

sources.title: What YC learned funding hard tech: back ambitious builders, raise money one miracle at a time
sources.originalTitle: What We Learned Funding Hard Tech
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell and PB look back on funding hard tech at YC (Ginkgo, Rigetti, Helion, OpenAI) and how it shapes Standard Capital. Back real builders with big ambition, expect less competition on outrageous ideas, and finance hard tech in stages by performing miracles rather than raising everything at once.

principles.text: Back great founders with real ambition; investors help build the company and raise capital, not supply the technical expertise.
principles.quote: as as always our belief is a lot of it comes down to having the right people, the right level of ambition, people who are real builders.

principles.text: Harder, more outrageous startups can face less competition and be more inspiring than low-ambition ones.
principles.quote: sometimes actually harder startups are like almost give you a better chance because it's so much more um inspiring, right? It's more exciting and and you have less competition.

principles.text: Few people can start a given hard tech company, so the founder-qualification bottleneck works as an inadvertent moat.
principles.quote: there were so few people that could start companies like that that it inadvertently was a moat.

principles.text: Funding a niche nobody else serves attracts the best founders, and they flock together, creating network effects.
principles.quote: because no one was funding those things, we we attracted a lot of the best founders.

principles.text: Hard tech founders need a clear path from today to the vision: ship a product now, scale, and prove yourself as you go.
principles.quote: You you have to you have to be able to see a clear path where we can deliver a product today, we can scale, we can raise much more you know, a certain amount of money, we can prove ourselves as we go

principles.text: Hard tech milestones are miracles, not revenue. Split financing into stages, each proving something, instead of raising it all at once.
principles.quote: You basically have to separate out each stage of capital and what you're going to prove with that fund raise um to get something that crazy financed.

sources.title: Dalton Caldwell on how YC startup advice holds up in the age of AI
sources.originalTitle: Startup Ideas Are Boring Now (Ex-YC Partner Dalton Caldwell)
sources.summary: Ex-YC partner Dalton Caldwell walks through classic YC advice (pick a non-obvious idea, build a simple MVP, talk to users, raise less, win by being unignorable) and how each updates with AI coding tools. Core theme: AI makes features and code cheap, so focus, direct user conversations and unconventional ideas matter more, not less.

principles.text: Obvious ideas on a new platform rarely become big outcomes; build something the new tech newly makes possible.
principles.quote: the really obvious App Store app ideas were kind of not good startups.

principles.text: Start from your unfair advantages and context, then apply them to the emerging technology.
principles.quote: you want to find the areas of context and advantages and then apply it to the emerging technology.

principles.text: With AI, code is easy for everyone; it must be paired with something inspired that delivers real user value.
principles.quote: anyone could write code some That is not enough. You have to combine that with something inspired, in my opinion, that delivers real value to users.

principles.text: Launch with one simple, explainable feature that solves a problem, then add rings around it. Cheap features don't change this.
principles.quote: do the hard thing first which is to make one feature that solves a problem for people and that they can explain back to you what the product is and why they want it

principles.text: Talk about what you're building publicly; most startups die from obscurity, not from being copied.
principles.quote: most startups die not because someone copied your idea, it's just because no one ever heard that you existed.

principles.text: Talk to users directly; 20-30 conversations beat thousands of ad-driven signups, and automating this loses nuance.
principles.quote: sitting down and talking to 20 or 30 people is going to give you more information about if you're on the right track or not than signing up 10,000 randos from Google Ads.

sources.title: Dalton Caldwell on pivoting: when, why and how to change your startup idea
sources.originalTitle: Dalton Caldwell - All About Pivoting
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell explains that pivoting is just changing your idea and should feel lightweight early on. He covers why founders pivot too late (loss aversion, politeness mistaken for traction), good and bad reasons to pivot, and a four-part scoring rubric for the next idea, illustrated with YC examples like Brex, Retool, Magic and Segment.

principles.text: Pivoting is just changing your idea; early on it should feel lightweight and happen constantly.
principles.quote: if you're not in a state where you're rapidly changing ideas or assumptions over and over and over again in quick succession, you are likely doing it wrong. You are likely moving too slow.

principles.text: Pivot because of opportunity cost: months of full-time effort without results is the strongest signal.
principles.quote: by working on something that's not working and you have evidence that it's not working, you are taking opportunity cost to not be doing something else.

principles.text: Don't confuse customer politeness with traction; polite feedback can keep you looping for years.
principles.quote: a lot of founders get confused about politeness and getting that confused with traction.

principles.text: A little traction is a trap; a total failure lets you move on immediately with no regrets.
principles.quote: I call it the uncanny valley of product market fit.

principles.text: Take several high-quality shots on goal; each full build-ship-learn iteration is another roll of the dice at product market fit.
principles.quote: it's much easier to be lucky when you get like half a dozen shots on goal than one

principles.text: Score a new idea on size, founder-market fit, ease of getting started, and early market feedback; easy-to-start ideas are undersold.
principles.quote: getting find an idea that's easy to get started with um is just as important as the idea itself.

sources.title: Dalton Caldwell on Standard Capital, AI moats and the Series A playbook
sources.originalTitle: Will AI kill every SaaS company? | Dalton Caldwell
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell explains how Standard Capital brings YC-style standardization to Series A: fixed public terms, founder-set price, no board seat. He also covers what stays defensible once AI can clone software, how to spot flash-in-the-pan growth, how to think about dilution at demo day, and what makes a tarpit idea.

principles.text: Standardize the deal and let the founder name the price, so you never negotiate against founders.
principles.quote: One of the worst parts um of being an investor from the YC partner perspective is negotiating against founders and not being aligned with them.

principles.text: Software that is merely hard to build is no longer a moat; look for marketplaces, network effects, data, scale or hard tech.
principles.quote: the moat of a lot of traditional SAS was that it was expensive or hard to build.

principles.text: Durable value means giving customers far more value than you charge, not subsidizing growth with ads.
principles.quote: the most enduring value is that you can durably help customers and give them more value than you are taking

principles.text: Face bad retention and revenue-retention data early instead of deferring the fix.
principles.quote: if your retention is bad, you are not creating value.

principles.text: Avoid stacking a bloated seed and a Series A within months; it is extremely dilutive.
principles.quote: raising a large slashbloated seed round and then raising a series A 6 months later, especially from a traditional VC, not us, and selling 15 or 20%. I think that's, dare I say, dumb.

principles.text: Hockey-stick revenue alone is not product-market fit; check sales cycle and retention quality before raising an A.
principles.quote: there's lots of companies that are extremely not, they don't have PMF, but they have a lot of revenue

sources.title: Dalton Caldwell (YC): don't die, pivot toward what you know, avoid tarpit ideas
sources.originalTitle: Lessons from 1,000+ YC startups: Resilience, tar pit ideas, pivoting, more | Dalton Caldwell (YC)
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell shares patterns from 1,000+ YC startups. Persistence beats cleverness, good pivots move closer to your expertise, tarpit ideas trap founders with false validation, and early founders should talk to customers in person instead of growth-hacking. He also covers why investors say no and the danger of over-delegating early.

principles.text: Keep going: nearly every big company had near-death moments where quitting looked rational.
principles.quote: there has to be this irrational you know intention to keep going even when the world tells you it's not working and you feel completely defeated and you likely have to go through this many times

principles.text: A good pivot moves closer to something you're an expert in and builds on what you learned from the prior idea.
principles.quote: usually a successful pivot gets warmer instead of Colder from what you're an expert at and somehow Builds on what you learned on the prior idea

principles.text: Pivot when you're out of growth ideas; stay the course while you still have many untried ones.
principles.quote: I would look at how many more ideas the founder has on how to make it grow like if it's not going well and you're out of ideas that is usually a good time to Pivot

principles.text: Tarpit ideas draw many founders with easy positive validation, so be wary of ideas everyone gravitates to.
principles.quote: part of being a true tarpit is that you can get good initial validation

principles.text: Talk to customers in person, spending 20-30% of your calendar on it, rather than hiding behind landing pages and ads.
principles.quote: look at your calendar and there should be you know 20 or 30% of your time that the calendar says something like customer meeting customer call

principles.text: Early-stage startups should skip growth hacking and analytics and get a first customer instead.
principles.quote: growth and growth hacking and doing all this analytics AB testing stuff um is a total waste of time for very early startups

sources.title: Dalton Caldwell on why music startups are a trap: lawsuits, blocked M&A, and dependence on others' content
sources.originalTitle: Dalton Caldwell - Founder of Picplz & Imeem @ Startup School 2010 (Part 2 of 2)
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell draws on his imeem experience to explain why building a startup on licensed music content is structurally dangerous. He covers when lawsuits arrive, why acquisitions break down, why labels act rationally, and why depending on someone else's content means you don't control your company.

principles.text: Success triggers lawsuits: rights holders only come after you once you have traffic and money.
principles.quote: look they're not gonna come talk to you until you have money until you're successful and uh that's the way it is

principles.text: If you depend on someone else's content to survive, you don't control the asset; you're a proxy for the content owner.
principles.quote: if you're dependent on someone else's content to survive you effectively are not in control of the asset it's not actually your company you're a proxy through the company

principles.text: Exits are nearly impossible in content-dependent businesses: no deals means legal liability, deals means the licensor can block a sale.
principles.quote: if you don't have deals no one's gonna buy you right that's they're not gonna buy some huge legal liabilities

principles.text: Check whether licensing deals transfer on acquisition; labels often hold a right of first refusal that works like a veto.
principles.quote: the labels have a right or first refusal to pull the deal if they don't like the acquisition

principles.text: Understand the counterparty's incentives: incumbents in a shrinking industry chase big wins, so small 'get big first, monetize later' pitches aren't worth their time.
principles.quote: they're trying to solve for these big wins they're not they're not trying to license a bunch of little people they need to find you know the touchdown pass the buzzer beater

principles.text: Short-term incentives drive bad system-level outcomes; people optimize for the next bonus, not long-term strategy.
principles.quote: it was a lot of people optimized optimizing for their own short-term benefit and doing what made complete sense that would create give them big bonuses at the end of the quarter right

sources.title: Tarpit ideas, the sequel: why seductive startup ideas keep failing and how new tech reopens them
sources.originalTitle: Tarpit Ideas: The Sequel
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel clarify that a tarpit idea is not just a bad idea. It is one many founders keep independently having, that earns lots of praise, and that keeps failing. The list is not static: new technology like LLMs can reopen old ideas, so founders should explain what changed and talk to users.

principles.text: A tarpit is a small subset of ideas that attract many founders and keep failing, not simply ideas you dislike.
principles.quote: tarpet ideas are a smallish set of ideas yes there's lots of ideas that are neither good nor bad they're just normal

principles.text: Too much positive feedback and a feeling that 'why does this not already exist' are warning signs, not validation.
principles.quote: if you're getting too much positive feedback if it feels like why does this already exist it seems so easy that's not like the shape of things that we see working

principles.text: The tarpit list is not static. New technology can make a previously failed idea workable, so explain what changed.
principles.quote: What I love to see is when a Founder can explain to me why the new technology might make something accomplishable that wasn't accomplishable before

principles.text: Ignoring that many people already tried and failed is a red flag. Do the research on prior attempts.
principles.quote: What I hate to see is a Founder that's not even acknowledging that like many people have tried and failed before

principles.text: Each new technology wave opens a new set of solvable problems, so re-explore what is now possible.
principles.quote: whatever current set of technology is available can address only a current set of problems and like some problems are going to fall outside of that set and every time there's a new chunk of Technology we have to re-explore

principles.text: To check whether your idea is a tarpit, talk to users and get a customer first.
principles.quote: when some of the people ask me oh is my idea tarpit I'll be like hey well have you talked to any users

sources.title: Dalton Caldwell: why music startups are a trap (opportunity cost, margins, minimums)
sources.originalTitle: Dalton Caldwell - Founder of Picplz & Imeem @ Startup School 2010 (Part 1 of 2)
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell, drawing on six years building imeem, walks through every music startup model (artist tools, download stores, ad-supported, subscription, unlicensed) and shows why the economics and deal structure usually fail. The durable lessons are opportunity cost, doing the unit-economics math early, and avoiding fixed contractual obligations.

principles.text: Weigh opportunity cost: years sunk into a hard market are years not spent on something better.
principles.quote: there's an opportunity cost when we decid to do a music start um and uh it's important to think about

principles.text: Easy traffic from free or unlicensed content is a false signal of product-market fit.
principles.quote: if you put up free income frees on a web server somewhere you'll get a lot of traffic and you'll feel really smart

principles.text: Avoid fixed minimum payments to partners; they remove your ability to pivot.
principles.quote: if you can't pivot when you're attached to something like this you can't pivot out of deals like this you're boned

principles.text: Run the margin math before picking a model: thin margins demand huge volume to fund even a tiny team.
principles.quote: at best you're going to get 20% margins

principles.text: Model subscription churn and what's left after costs before building; monthly churn and licensing eat most of the price.
principles.quote: you charge 10 bucks a month uh you're going to face 10% monthly turn of people unsubscribing

principles.text: The real obstacle in a hard market is often structural (legal, licensing), not the people involved.
principles.quote: to me it's not about the people it's about the structures

sources.title: Standard Capital: Dalton Caldwell on rebuilding the Series A with YC's seed-stage playbook
sources.originalTitle: Inside Standard Capital: New $425M Series A Fund, Explained
sources.summary: Dalton explains why he launched Standard Capital with Paul Buchheit and Brian Berg: apply the YC seed model (short application, standard terms, founder-set price, fast answer) to the Series A. He argues fundraising is a time sink, valuation is made up, and founder peer groups beat board seats.

principles.text: Fundraising is a distraction from the business; spend as little time on it as possible.
principles.quote: fundraising is a waste of time don't do it like to do it as do it in as short of amount of time as possible.

principles.text: Design the process so the founder's time cost is minimal and the downside is near zero.
principles.quote: the whole point is to have the time cost to a founder to be minimal.

principles.text: Publish standard terms up front so founders know the deal before applying, not after they have said yes.
principles.quote: you'll know exactly what the deal is before you apply instead of it being this opaque thing

principles.text: Early-stage valuation is made-up numbers, so let the founder name their own price.
principles.quote: There's no equation. Everyone just makes up numbers.

principles.text: Replace board seats with a curated founder peer group; the best advice comes from other operators.
principles.quote: the best advice you're going to get from as a founder is from other founders and from peers that you respect.

principles.text: Help each founder find the one idea where they have the most unfair advantages.
principles.quote: I believe that every person has like a perfect idea for them

sources.title: Where great startup ideas come from: Airbnb, Coinbase and Stripe
sources.originalTitle: Where Do Great Startup Ideas Come From? – Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel unpack why Airbnb, Coinbase and Stripe worked. Each entered a market with bad incumbents, built something 10x better, was told by experts it was a dumb idea, and found the market bigger than they first thought. The lessons: ignore incumbents and non-user experts, build for users you know, and be careful with market-size math.

principles.text: Don't be scared off by an existing product. If its users hate it, a 10x better version is the opening.
principles.quote: you shouldn't give a [ __ ] if there's an existing product in the market if you're a user of that product or your friends or users of that product and they all hate it

principles.text: Ignore experts who aren't users and have never felt the pain of the existing product.
principles.quote: you should not give a [ __ ] if most of the people around you who you believe are experts don't think this is a good idea especially you shouldn't care if they're not going to be users

principles.text: Be skeptical of your own market size math. A 10x better product unlocks use cases you can't foresee.
principles.quote: be very careful about pretending that you know how big the market could be it turns out with so many of these transformational technologies there are use cases you can't dream of

principles.text: If your smart technical friends all complain about the same thing, that's a strong hint for an idea.
principles.quote: if all of your smart technical friends are complaining about the same thing maybe it's a real problem

principles.text: Stripe won developers by building what a programmer would want: beautiful site and docs, plus a scarce beta invite.
principles.quote: constantly ask themselves and push themselves to say what would i want or what would it what would a programmer want

principles.text: Pricing high can signal a real insight. Stripe was the most expensive option and people were still desperate for it.
principles.quote: they didn't give it away for free they didn't price it comparably they made it more expensive and people were still desperate to use it

sources.title: Why top investors secretly love YC: read incentives and judge investors by what they do, not say
sources.originalTitle: The Secret That Silicon Valley's Top Investors All Share
sources.summary: Dalton and Michael Seibel explain the gap between investors dismissing YC publicly and funding YC companies constantly. The lesson for founders: understand each investor's incentives (first check, ownership, price) and weigh actions over talk.

principles.text: Investors say 'too early' when a startup lacks signal; a credible filter like YC supplies that signal.
principles.quote: too early just means there's not enough signal that this is one of these epic standout companies which is their job to invest in

principles.text: Packaged, pre-filtered deal flow is valuable to investors because they can only do so many deals.
principles.quote: the average VC only does one deal a year maybe two deals a year

principles.text: Investors want to be your first check and dislike you talking to many investors in parallel; talk to many anyway.
principles.quote: it's scary when your customers first talk to someone else before you because you can get disintermediated in the future

principles.text: Seed funds want big ownership at low prices, so they have a built-in incentive to discourage you from doing YC.
principles.quote: your job is to get a big ownership in the company and then try to get the VCS to fund them in the next round

principles.text: Understand the incentives of whoever is marketing or advising you; they are running a business too.
principles.quote: the people who are marketing to you are running their businesses and those businesses have Dynamics you understand those Dynamics

principles.text: Discount advice from investors who aren't offering money; take real offers seriously and judge by actions, not tweets.
principles.quote: maybe you should spend a little bit more time looking at what people do rather than what they say or they meme or they tweet

sources.title: Dalton Caldwell on balancing optimism and pessimism: avoiding magical thinking as a founder
sources.originalTitle: The Two Mindsets That Can KILL Your Startup
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel describe the two failure modes of founder mindset: too pessimistic (quitting after one bad signal) and too optimistic (magical thinking detached from how the world works). Dalton argues founders must hold both views at once, stay rooted in reality, and not expect funding, hires or trends to rescue an unproven startup.

principles.text: Founders need to be both optimistic and pessimistic; extremes in either direction lead to failure.
principles.quote: the fact is you need to be both optimistic and pessimistic okay and if you're too far on either extreme you are going to fail

principles.text: Test your mindset by imagining your employees: a leader who doesn't believe is bad, but wildly optimistic plans destroy credibility and trust.
principles.quote: a good leader is an optimist they believe if they don't believe they're a horrible leader

principles.text: Magical thinking is a poor grasp of how the world actually works; ground yourself in real cause and effect.
principles.quote: the whole concept of magical thinking is a poor grasp of how the world actually works

principles.text: Raising money from famous investors doesn't remove problems; don't switch off your brain after a funding round.
principles.quote: just because you raise a bunch of money from important famous people does not mean all problems no longer exist

principles.text: Don't expect a marketing or sales hire to solve your biggest unsolved problem pre-product-market fit.
principles.quote: if we just hire a marketing person a sales person this person they will come in and solve the biggest problem inside of the company especially pre-product market fit

principles.text: The best founders hold conflicting ideas at once, handling bad news and wins without freaking out or losing touch with reality.
principles.quote: the best founders have techniques and they can do it i think and they can like be really good at it

sources.title: Why investors can't fix your company: match advice to the advisor's background
sources.originalTitle: Why Investors Can’t Fix Your Company – Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel walk through types of investors (finance, big-company exec, non-tech entrepreneur, junior, influencer, founder, young scout) and how each one's background skews their advice. The takeaway is that nobody, YC included, can tell a founder how to win, so founders must own the outcome and use advisors selectively.

principles.text: An investor's advice reflects their background; a finance person's fix is usually more money.
principles.quote: when all you have is a hammer everything's a nail and so if what you know is money the solutions usually involve money

principles.text: Scaling a successful product is a different muscle from getting the first users at a startup.
principles.quote: it's a very different muscle to build scaling instagram post acquisition if you were on that team than being getting the first 100 users when you were the founder of instagram

principles.text: Be wary of advice that is just an advisor's autobiography; good advisors condense many founders' learnings.
principles.quote: a lot of my advice was heavily based on my personal experience and it only it took years of me working at yc to sort of break out of that trap

principles.text: Even YC's standard advice doesn't fit every case, so give it carefully.
principles.quote: the best yc partners are very careful with how forcefully we give the yc advice

principles.text: Founders who made it took accountability and didn't blindly follow anyone, YC included.
principles.quote: they took personal accountability that they're the ones who are gonna have to make it work

principles.text: Advisors without a financial stake give more honest feedback.
principles.quote: you can get a lot more honesty out of somebody when they're not financially incentivized to kind of blow smoke up your ass

sources.title: Setting goals before product-market fit: get users who love it, skip the graphs
sources.originalTitle: How to Set Goals Before Product-Market Fit
sources.summary: Dalton and Michael argue pre-PMF startups should ignore growth graphs and weekly growth targets, and focus on a ladder of real users who love the product (1, 10, 50, 100). Gmail and Stripe show great products start slow and obsessively served. Building for investors instead of users is a trap.

principles.text: With zero or few users, skip the graphs. Get something that someone loves first.
principles.quote: Don't even worry about graphs and charts and weekly growth. Just get something that someone loves.

principles.text: Use a user-count ladder as your goal: 1 real user, then 10, 50, 100 who love it. Graduate to graphs at 100.
principles.quote: if you could get 100 users or customers that love you, that is an awesome goal, and that's when I would start to graduate to graphs.

principles.text: Growth is the result of doing many things right, not the cause of a working company. Don't doctor metrics to hit a target.
principles.quote: growing 7% week over week is a result of doing a lot of things right. Whereas they think it is the cause of the company working.

principles.text: Don't build a startup to convince investors. Your customer is the user, not the investor.
principles.quote: If you start thinking this way that your entire startup is a product made to convince investors, you will not win.

principles.text: Great products often start tiny: Gmail had under 100 users for months, Stripe took two years to launch publicly. Test your startup assumptions against your favorite companies' early stories.
principles.quote: It was invite-only, it was beta-only. They built it for themselves for a side product and they only added customers super slow.

principles.text: Quantify the benefit customers get (like dollars earned), not just time spent. Early customer closeness, like Stripe's founders messaging customers daily, builds loyalty.
principles.quote: can you quantify the actual benefit of the customer as opposed to just time with you or that kind of stuff.

sources.title: Dalton Caldwell: Why low ambition kills venture-backed startups
sources.originalTitle: Low Ambition is Killing Your Startup
sources.summary: Dalton and Michael Seibel argue that aiming small is the hidden killer of venture-backed startups, because big missions attract customers, hires and investors who care. They stress that ambition must come with a simple, credible pitch rooted in real knowledge, and warn against funding-cycle noise and scenesters.

principles.text: Pair big ambition with a pitch built on intuitive, credible logical leaps.
principles.quote: a pitch where the logical leaps you are making are intuitive and that you are credible at making those logical leaps.

principles.text: Root ambition in things you actually know, and keep the leap of faith small.
principles.quote: you have to root it in things that you know about and make very simple low leap of faith arguments on how you'll be able to do it.

principles.text: Tell your ambitious story to everyone, constantly; it recruits team, money and believers.
principles.quote: And that simple story that is that ambitious and clearly he just told everyone that.

principles.text: Funding trends in the market can warp your sense of what a good idea is.
principles.quote: if you're keeping score on what's raising money, you can get really warped ideas about what good is.

principles.text: Pick ideas by their potential impact, not by whether they can raise a seed round.
principles.quote: Like whether it can raise a seed round is not the KPI.

principles.text: If you can't make your startup ambitious, work somewhere ambitious first; a low-ambition idea is a tarpit.
principles.quote: If you burn years of your life on something that you think is a waste of time in your heart of hearts that is a true tarpit.

sources.title: How to find unique AI startup ideas: look in the discard bin, not at what just got funded
sources.originalTitle: How To Get Unique AI Startup Ideas
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel argue that with AI tools making building cheap, the scarce thing is a genuinely unique idea. Copying funded companies or VC consensus gives derivative ideas; look at ideas others discarded, work from your own weirdness, and expect people to call it bad.

principles.text: When tools make building easy, the real bottleneck is having a good idea, not shipping it.
principles.quote: you can crank out anything. And so, the bottleneck is less building the thing, it's actually um having an idea.

principles.text: Don't hunt for an idea nobody has thought of; find one everyone has thought of and dismissed as bad.
principles.quote: instead of trying to find something no one's ever thought of, find something that everyone's thought of and thinks is bad.

principles.text: Late-stage VC sizing rules (huge TAM) filter out truly unique early ideas and push you toward derivative ones.
principles.quote: trying to take these like late-stage investor advice things and apply them to startup ideas, only a small number of things would meet that bar.

principles.text: Non-conformists generate unique ideas naturally; their harder job is filtering which idea deserves their time.
principles.quote: Those people tend to do well with startups because they don't actually have any problems coming up with unique ideas.

principles.text: People who excel at reading consensus struggle most to produce unique ideas, since the skill is trained out of them.
principles.quote: people that are really good at calibrating and triangulating consensus, those tend to be people that have the hardest time coming up with unique ideas

principles.text: Don't seek approval from authority figures (including podcasters and investors) when choosing what to build.
principles.quote: don't be approval seeking from authority figures if you want actually have unique ideas.

sources.title: Startup Problems Growth Doesn't Solve: Unit Economics, Moats, Vision and Hiring
sources.originalTitle: Startup Problems Growth Doesn't Solve
sources.summary: Growth fixes many startup problems like fundraising and burnout, but fast growth can hide serious ones. Dalton and Michael list what founders should probe when growing fast: unit economics at each scale, defensibility, vision, real customer usage and hiring quality.

principles.text: Faster growth doesn't fix uneconomic unit economics; don't assume economies of scale without probing them.
principles.quote: But by and large, just growing faster doesn't mean you're going to solve uneconomic issues.

principles.text: Re-check unit economics like CAC at every order of magnitude, since they often change as you scale.
principles.quote: the assumptions around unit economics at small scale need to be reassessed at every order of magnitude scale because oftentimes they change.

principles.text: Fast growth is not a moat. Ask what stops a copycat from taking your customers.
principles.quote: we've seen people grow really, really, really fast and have no clue how to make it defensible

principles.text: Be your own biggest critic when things go well, because nobody else will do that work.
principles.quote: when things are going well, you have to be your own biggest critic.

principles.text: A clear picture of what the company should become matters even with a hockey-stick graph; assume a competitor has one.
principles.quote: I think the folks with the clearest picture are probably going to win.

principles.text: Growth doesn't prove you solve the customer's problem. Check whether people actually use what was sold.
principles.quote: just because you're growing fast doesn't mean you are solving your customer's problem.

sources.title: Leverage: how founders win at fundraising, sales, hiring and PR
sources.originalTitle: How Founders Win at Fundraising, Sales, and Hiring
sources.summary: Dalton and Michael frame every startup negotiation around leverage: do you bring more value than you ask for, and could you walk away? Growth and a deep pipeline beat pitch decks, negotiation tricks and press. The pre-work is where the win happens.

principles.text: Leverage means bringing more value than you ask for; investors, customers and hires are not there to support you like teachers.
principles.quote: Do you bring something of value? Are you asking for more value than you can offer or are you delivering more value than you're asking for?

principles.text: Fundraising is won by growth and proof points, not deck polish; a bad fundraiser with traction beats a great one without.
principles.quote: the way to be very effective at fundraising is to be growing so quickly and have so many proof points that your startup is working

principles.text: Some investors string founders along for months as a free option, draining the time you need to build the inflection point.
principles.quote: The dark game theory is that the reason a lot of founders will get strung along for months is the investor is trying to see if they do start growing

principles.text: In sales, high leverage is heavy inbound so you can be picky; never depend on one deal, and keep doing outreach during a hot deal.
principles.quote: high leverage is that you have so much customer inbound that you can be picky and choosy.

principles.text: Hiring leverage comes from a deep pipeline; most founders have too few candidates at every stage.
principles.quote: I think when I'm debugging um founders hiring pipeline, the biggest issue is they don't have a pipeline.

principles.text: Treat hiring like sales: put in comparable effort, and move fast on good candidates, even handing a signed offer letter at the end of the last interview.
principles.quote: the amount of like emotional energy you have to put into hiring is on the level as getting customers because you're basically selling a job at your company.

sources.title: Dalton Caldwell: Why you should keep working on your startup through the trough of sorrow
sources.originalTitle: Should You Keep Working on Your Startup?
sources.summary: Dalton and Michael argue most startups die of suicide, not homicide, and that quitting guarantees failure. Failing early is the natural state, success usually takes longer than founders think, and you should quit only once your hypothesis is clearly answered or for money or health reasons.

principles.text: Giving up guarantees failure; most startups die from founders running out of hope, not from competitors.
principles.quote: I think that um most startups die of suicide than homicide. And that running out of hope is the is the thing that causes people to give up.

principles.text: Struggling is the normal default state of a startup. Others' success looks faster than it really was.
principles.quote: The natural state of startups is that they are failing.

principles.text: Roads to success are mostly longer than you think. Check the real timelines of companies you admire.
principles.quote: there are a lot of roads to success, and most of them are longer than you think.

principles.text: Don't repeat year one forever by pivoting before you've learned anything real. Stay long enough to know something.
principles.quote: I think that like one of the things that I see a lot of founders do is like repeat year one over and over again.

principles.text: Quit only for real reasons (out of money, health), or once you've learned your hypothesis is wrong, not because progress is slower than expected.
principles.quote: I think that the failure mode is to quit before you actually have clear information about whether your hypothesis was right.

principles.text: Startups trade money EV for agency. If you only want max expected value with minimal risk, don't found one.
principles.quote: You're making a trade where you're giving yourself more agency for more risk.

sources.title: Dear Mark Zuckerberg: Why building on ad-funded platforms is a trap and infrastructure-style platforms win
sources.originalTitle: Dear Mark Zuckerberg
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell's 2012 open letter recounts Facebook executives pitching an acqui-hire to neutralize his competing app, and uses it to argue that ad-funded platforms turn on their developers. He lays out platform risk and his thesis that future social platforms should act like infrastructure with clear business models.

principles.text: Building on an ad-funded platform carries huge platform risk; the owner may compete with you or squeeze you.
principles.quote: Personally speaking, I am resolved to never write another line of code for rotten-to-the-core “platforms” like Facebook or Twitter. Lesson learned.

principles.text: Ad-revenue pressure pushes platforms to mess with users and developers, and once they start they rarely stop.
principles.quote: Once you start down the slippery-slope of messing with developers and users, I don’t have any confidence you will stop.

principles.text: Future platforms should behave like infrastructure, as smaller interoperable players with clear, sustainable business models.
principles.quote: I believe that a number of smaller, interoperable social platforms with a clear, sustainable business models will usurp you.

principles.text: Judge a platform by the value its ecosystem generates, not the value the platform captures for itself.
principles.quote: Platforms are judged by the value generated by their ecosystem, not by the value the platforms directly capture.

principles.text: A business model misaligned with users and developers is a structural flaw, regardless of how good the people inside are.
principles.quote: I just think you constructed a business that has financial motivations that are not in-line with users & developers.

sources.title: What Twitter could have been: why an open realtime API beats an ad-funded media business
sources.originalTitle: What Twitter could have been
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell argues Twitter's fork between becoming a realtime API platform and building an AdWords-style ad business was a strategic mistake. Choosing ads forced Twitter to own all screen real-estate, kill third-party clients and lock down data, shrinking its potential versus an ecosystem play.

principles.text: Platforms with powerful APIs can become fundamental infrastructure, a bigger prize than a single consumer app.
principles.quote: I realized that Twitter, because of their API, actually was a real-time protocol to connect various services in a novel way.

principles.text: Your business model dictates your platform behavior: an ad business must control all the screen real-estate users see.
principles.quote: If you are building an advertising/media business, it would then follow that you need to own all of the screen real-estate that users see.

principles.text: Ad-based models push you to kill third-party clients and lock down data to control the content, which destroys the ecosystem.
principles.quote: The next logical step would be to kill all 3rd-party clients, and lock down the data in the global firehose in order to control the “content”.

principles.text: An open, API-centric strategy can enable an ecosystem more powerful than a closed network, so don't settle for a good outcome if a far bigger one was available.
principles.quote: I believe an API-centric Twitter could have enabled an ecosystem far more powerful than what Facebook is today.

principles.text: Success today doesn't mean you realized your potential; ask whether years of talent and capital produced what they could have.
principles.quote: But is the service we think of as Twitter today really the Twitter from a few years ago living up to its full potential?

principles.text: Betraying your developer ecosystem erodes trust and long-term value; strategic fork decisions early determine the company's ceiling.
principles.quote: Nowadays, every time I get a K-Mart ad in my feed, or see wonky behavior in the official clients, or see Twitter drop another bomb on their developer ecosystem, I think back and wish the pro-API guys won that internal battle.

sources.title: Why App.net bet on paid, ad-free services: Dalton Caldwell's case against ad-supported products
sources.originalTitle: Announcing an audacious proposal
sources.summary: Dalton argues that services too important to their users (SourceForge/GitHub, Dropbox) shouldn't be ad-supported, and that paid, profitable stewards build better products. Drawing on his imeem failure, he proposes a Kickstarter-style campaign requiring $500K / ~10,000 backers as critical mass before App.net launches a paid realtime feed service.

principles.text: Services that are too important to users shouldn't be ad-supported; charge for them instead.
principles.quote: the services provided by SourceForge/Github are **too important to its users to be ad-supported**.

principles.text: A paid, profitable steward builds a better product than an ad-supported one, because the team improves the service instead of extracting pennies.
principles.quote: Github is apparently profitable, and it sounds like the people that work there spend their time trying to make the best service possible, _as opposed to spending their time trying to extract additional pennies out of their users_.

principles.text: Free services with vague business models trap founders: growth balloons costs, forcing a sale, ads, or endless fundraising.
principles.quote: Because the hosting bills and payroll balloon as the service grows, founders are left with a very difficult decision to make.

principles.text: Don't run an important service on hand-wavy promises of future monetization; it fails users, employees and trust.
principles.quote: Running a service that is important to people with some sort of hand-wavy platitudes about someday launching a “new form of advertising” is not OK.

principles.text: Pre-validate willingness to pay with an all-or-nothing campaign that only takes money at a defined critical mass.
principles.quote: We will only accept money for this financially sustainable, ad-free service if we hit what I believe is critical mass.

principles.text: A small base of 10,000 committed users can be a powerful starting position, so target the users who most want the product.
principles.quote: A search engine whose users consisted of the top 10,000 hackers and no one else would be in a very powerful position despite its small size, just as Google was when it was that size.

sources.title: Critical mass vs network effects: why growing a community at all costs backfires
sources.originalTitle: Critical mass vs network effects
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell argues that raw user count is a vanity metric. Communities need critical mass, but low-quality signups can destroy value (anti-network effects). He uses Orkut, Facebook suggested users and Twitter's asymmetric follow plus global feed to show how to seed a small high-quality core and scale without driving it away.

principles.text: More users does not automatically make a community more valuable; the wrong signups can drive away the core.
principles.quote: Wait a second, the conventional wisdom is that more users makes a community more valuable? Well, not in this case. US traffic and usage dropped like a rock.

principles.text: "Grow users at all costs" is VC dogma, tied to the assumption that consumer products must be free and ad-supported.
principles.quote: This is one of the reasons that “grow your userbase as fast as possible at all costs” has become VC dogma for consumer Internet. I can absolutely understand the reasoning behind this, but dogma is still dogma.

principles.text: Big follower counts built from suggested or random users are a vanity numbers game, not real audience quality.
principles.quote: aren’t these big numbers a superficial numbers-game more than, well, _quality_?

principles.text: Anti-network effects: past critical mass, each added signup can reduce value if the core community that created it gets marginalized and leaves.
principles.quote: Anti-network effects occur when a community which has already achieved critical mass begins to _lose_ value with each additional signup. The reason is that the core community that created the value to begin with starts to get marginalized and leaves.

principles.text: Seed a small, dedicated group of interesting people with asymmetric follows and a global feed, then scale; early users tune their own feeds as it grows.
principles.quote: if you launch with a small, dedicated group of interesting people that can asymmetrically follow each other, along with a global feed of _all_ content posted, you can feel like you are the member of an interesting and vibrant community.

principles.text: Asymmetric follows keep strangers from dumping unwanted messages on your content, helping protect community quality at scale.
principles.quote: Strangers can choose to follow you, and @-reply to you, but it doesn’t feel like they are “putting” their troubling messages on your content.

sources.title: Why platforms shouldn't be ad-supported: Dalton Caldwell's case for paid services over free media models
sources.originalTitle: Fred Wilson is wrong about Free
sources.summary: Dalton rebuts Fred Wilson's defense of "free" by arguing that platforms (APIs others build businesses on) are different from media, and that ad-supported models push platform owners to control content and eventually compete with or crush developers. He argues digital services are easy to monetize while digital content is not, so communications platforms should charge users.

principles.text: Platforms that developers build on should not be ad-supported; free can still be right for other businesses.
principles.quote: My arguments are that _platforms_ should not be ad-supported. I never said that “free” is the wrong business model for everyone.

principles.text: Building on a platform is a foundational risk: the owner can degrade you, shut you down, or compete with you.
principles.quote: Building on top of a platform is a foundational risk, and if your platform decided one day that it doesn’t like what you are doing, or likes what you are doing so much they want to compete with you, it’s Very Bad.

principles.text: Set the business model so third-party developers never need to hedge against their platform partner turning on them.
principles.quote: I’m trying to build a platform where the core values and associated business model are set up to ensure no 3rd-party developer will need to hedge against the possibility that, one day, their platform partner will decide to make them their “bitch”.

principles.text: Control-and-scarcity business models create incentives that crush innovation, even when the people involved are good.
principles.quote: The problem was, their control and scarcity-based business model was/is intractably flawed. The vast majority of innovations created by digital music startups will be crushed because the labels have a fundamental financial incentive to do so.

principles.text: A paid, service-based model is more open than an ad-supported one: content is just bits passing through, not the product.
principles.quote: In other words, content is not king– it’s just bits passing through our system, at the behest of our customers.

principles.text: Digital services are valuable and easy to monetize; digital content is not. Treat communications platforms as services, not media.
principles.quote: In my view of the world, digital “services” are valuable/easy to monetize, and digital “content” is not.

sources.title: Why Sequoia's 'RIP Good Times' warning was good faith, not fearmongering
sources.originalTitle: RIP Good Times: Silicon Valley's Cuban Missile Crisis
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell recounts attending Sequoia's 2008 'RIP Good Times' meeting as a portfolio CEO, weeks after Lehman collapsed. He argues the warning was sincere, not manipulative, and that the financial system was in a Cuban Missile Crisis moment. Mostly historical perspective with light lessons on crisis response.

principles.text: In a crisis, trust investors' actions over press narratives: the partners' warning was a good-faith attempt to help founders.
principles.quote: I was there, I looked in the partners’ eyes, they weren’t bluffing. They were trying to help us.

principles.text: Being wrong about a warning doesn't make the warning bad; act on the best information you have and be glad the worst case didn't happen.
principles.quote: That being said, I am glad that presentation ended up being wrong, just as I am glad the Cuban Missile Crisis did not turn into a full-blown nuclear war.

principles.text: Investors who share proprietary knowledge and tactical instructions with portfolio CEOs are giving founders an edge in a downturn.
principles.quote: I don’t see how Sequoia’s efforts to communicate a (somewhat sanitized) version of the knowledge they had to their portfolio CEOs, and to provide actionable tactical instructions to us, could be perceived of as anything but good faith.

principles.text: Context gets lost over time; judging a decision in hindsight, without the fear and uncertainty of the moment, distorts the story.
principles.quote: I am of the opinion that some of the context of that particular event has been lost.

sources.title: Dalton Caldwell on organizational complexity: how to manage it as a startup grows
sources.originalTitle: Some thoughts on organizational complexity
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell argues that complexity is both a cost and a necessity. Large companies need it to ship complex products but it breeds inward-focused politics. Startups should stay simple and focused, then add internal complexity deliberately as traffic and revenue demand it, without overextending.

principles.text: Don't assume success with a simple model will scale up smoothly to more complex real-world conditions.
principles.quote: don’t assume that a successful AI project which utilizes a simple model will seamlessly scale up to more complex circumstances.

principles.text: Large companies need organizational complexity to ship complex products, but it breeds inward-focused politics.
principles.quote: Apple is very complex organization… but that complexity is what allows them to ship very complex products.

principles.text: As companies grow, resources drift toward internal issues rather than customers; don't ship your org chart.
principles.quote: It would seem that the larger a company gets, the more the company tends to allocate resources towards inwardly focused (as opposed to outwardly focused) issues.

principles.text: Focus and simplicity are really complexity management; doing too many things makes the org mirror that mess.
principles.quote: If a company tries to do too many things at once, the company org chart and workflow will naturally begin to model that complexity.

principles.text: Use tools like AWS, outsourced HR and Stripe to keep a startup's internal model simple and easy to change.
principles.quote: Simple models are the easiest to understand and modify on the fly.

principles.text: Add internal complexity deliberately when demand grows (traffic, revenue); refusing to build support or accounting systems in the name of simplicity is a mistake.
principles.quote: A founder probably shouldn’t say: “I believe in simplicity and focus, therefore we will have no systems in place to handle accounting or customer support.”

sources.title: Zen & the art of startup advice: why advice contradicts itself and how to filter it
sources.originalTitle: Zen & the art of startup advice
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell argues that startup advice blogposts are self-contradictory when synthesized, much like the cold-reading "rainbow ruse." Succeeding means being comfortable holding contradictory information, distrusting black-and-white thinkers, and keeping emotions level in good times and bad.

principles.text: Startup advice, taken together, is deeply self-contradictory, so it is less useful than it feels.
principles.quote: if you tried to synthesize all of the available advice into a single coherent framework, you would quickly realize that the aggregate “advice framework” is deeply self-contradictory.

principles.text: Succeeding in startups and life requires being comfortable holding contradictory information.
principles.quote: nothing is black-and-white, and in fact, much of succeeding in life consists of being comfortable sitting with contradictory information

principles.text: Anxiety drives people to crave simple linear narratives and tidy formulas that explain success.
principles.quote: Anxious people eat this stuff up… anything to cure the squishy uncertainty in the pit of their stomachs.

principles.text: Keep your advice filter sharp: distrust black-and-white thinkers and oversimplified explanations of complex events.
principles.quote: Beware of black-and-white thinkers. Beware of people that present very simple narratives as the explanation of incredibly complex events. Don’t take anything you read too literally.

principles.text: Everyone feels uncertain; some just hide it better, so don't compare your insides to others' outsides.
principles.quote: Realize that _everyone_ feels this way, it’s just that some work harder than others to cover it up.

principles.text: Use a paired mantra to smooth emotional swings, since euphoria is as dangerous as despair.
principles.quote: Things are much worse than they seem, also, things are much better than they seem.

sources.title: The Edifice Complex: why long-term real estate obligations kill startups
sources.originalTitle: The Edifice Complex, a silent killer
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell argues that bad real estate deals were a hidden killer of dotcom-era companies. Companies that over-leased or built showpiece offices could not wind down in a downturn, while Google and Facebook stayed in cheap space until they could afford better. Lesson: protect your ability to cut burn.

principles.text: Long-term real estate obligations are inflexible and can sink a company when cash gets tight.
principles.quote: significant long-term real estate obligations are a one-way ticket to bankruptcy court

principles.text: Survival in a downturn depends on how well you can wind down fixed obligations, especially real estate.
principles.quote: one of the clear dividing lines between who lived and died in the dotcom shakeout was who could most effectively wind down their real estate deals

principles.text: Even a great brand can't save a company whose bad real estate deals make it unfixable.
principles.quote: the extent that bad real estate deals made the company unfixable

principles.text: Don't lease space to signal growth. Leases are not proof of revenue or headcount growth.
principles.quote: they did this to demonstrate growth in amount of square footage they leased as a leading indicator of revenue and headcount growth

principles.text: Stay frugal while you're winning: Google started in cheap, crappy space and Facebook in small scattered offices.
principles.quote: Google leased a bunch of cheap/crappy real estate next to the freeway in Mountain View

principles.text: Hot companies are tempted to build or buy showpiece buildings; resist the 'edifice complex' and keep cash-burn levers available.
principles.quote: hot companies building/buying huge buildings and decking them with expensive furnishings and signage as “the edifice complex”

sources.title: Two Apple moves behind iOS: Windows iPods and Moore's-law market segmentation
sources.originalTitle: Two brilliant moves that helped create the Apple iOS powerhouse
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell argues two underappreciated Apple tactics built its mobile dominance. Windows-compatible iPods co-opted the Windows userbase and made desktop OS irrelevant, and selling older iPhone models cheaply segmented the market off a single product line, which large rivals struggle to copy because of corporate inertia.

principles.text: Co-opt a rival's installed base by making your product work in their ecosystem, even when it feels off-brand.
principles.quote: By casually co-opting the Windows userbase, Apple made **Windows desktop marketshare irrelevant in the mobile-centric world that would soon come into being.**

principles.text: A first product purchase can be a wedge: the iPod was many people's first Apple device and paved the way for later product lines.
principles.quote: But Windows-compatible iPods paved the way for the iPhone. For iOS. For the iPad.

principles.text: Segment the market off one product line by letting older models become the cheaper tier, instead of building separate products.
principles.quote: Apple is doing market segmentation off of a single product line!

principles.text: One team focused on one great product lets Moore's law turn today's flagship into tomorrow's entry-level device, with no retooling.
principles.quote: They put all of their energy into building the single greatest product they can. Without expending any effort, they simply let Moore’s law transform today’s great product into tomorrow’s entry-level device.

principles.text: Price is a powerful lever: a product nobody could sell at list price flew off shelves at $99.
principles.quote: Lo and behold, the product that they couldn’t sell to save their lives **flew off the shelves** at the $99 price point.

principles.text: Large incumbents often can't copy strategies like this because of corporate inertia: org charts, fiefdoms and existing revenue lines resist consolidation.
principles.quote: However, if I had to take a single guess, I would guess _corporate inertia_.

sources.title: The music industry vs AOL: why risk-shifting licensing deals beat bold bets on safety, not on upside
sources.originalTitle: The music industry vs AOL
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell compares AOL's high-risk pivot away from dial-up access with the music industry's strategy of wiring every licensing deal for success. The labels push product and execution risk onto licensees, so they don't care which service wins. It's a lens on who holds risk in a business model and which outcome you optimize for.

principles.text: Declining cash cows force a choice: make bold bets yourself, or push risk onto partners via deal structure.
principles.quote: AOL strategy to save themselves from a dying legacy business has been to make longshot bets. These longshot bets keep the risk/rewards on management’s shoulders.

principles.text: Licensing-based incumbents engineer deals so product and execution risk sits far from their core business.
principles.quote: The music industry strategy has been to utilize financial engineering in order to push product & execution risk off as far away from their core business as possible.

principles.text: When every deal is wired for success, no single partner's outcome matters; only the supply of new deals does.
principles.quote: If every deal is wired, it doesn’t matter how successful any individual license-holder is.

principles.text: A platform that earns on every licensee is indifferent to which licensee wins, like Exxon with gas stations.
principles.quote: the music industry cares as much about which music service “wins” as ExxonMobil cares which gas station chain wins.

principles.text: Bold strategic moves draw criticism because they can fail; the right strategy depends on the outcome you optimize for.
principles.quote: Which strategy is better? I suppose it depends on what outcome you are optimizing for.

sources.title: Letter to myself in late 2008: how to survive a crisis, from imeem's CEO
sources.originalTitle: Letter to myself in late 2008
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell writes to his 2008 self, then CEO of imeem with ~90 employees and high burn. The lessons: stop counting on fundraising, use the cash you have, renegotiate every contract, cut once and deeply to reach profitability, and make decisions yourself instead of averaging advice.

principles.text: Stop planning around future fundraising; work with the cash you actually have.
principles.quote: Stop thinking or talking about future fundraising. This entire line of thinking will lead to lots of wasted cycles.

sources.title: Startup childhood: why tiny startups aren't Google in miniature
sources.originalTitle: Startup childhood
sources.summary: Dalton Caldwell argues that founders should treat pre-PMF startups like children, not miniature adults. Early-stage companies should prioritize differently than late-stage ones, and everyone around the company should be honest about whether PMF has been reached.

principles.text: Don't run your startup as a miniature version of your dream end-state company.
principles.quote: Often, those middle steps are conceptualized by the founders as consisting of them r_unning their dream endstate company but in miniaturized form_. This mental model can be very counterproductive.

principles.text: Prioritize differently pre-PMF than post-PMF; don't copy late-stage structures too early.
principles.quote: A few examples of things that could be questionable at a very early stage startup but you would expect at a late stage startup: hiring a full org chart with all functions a late stage company would have, shipping multiple products at the same time under different names, many tiers of management and job titles, etc.

principles.text: Use product-market fit, not fundraising size, as the dividing line between early and mature startup stages.
principles.quote: I believe that the most helpful way to differentiate between pre and post "childhood" stages is by whether the startup has achieved product-market fit (PMF).

principles.text: Don't conflate fundraising success or valuation with PMF; that conflation destroys value for everyone involved.
principles.quote: The conflation of fundraising success, valuation, and PMF status can be value-destructive to all of the stakeholders involved.

principles.text: Raising big money ahead of traction creates a shared fiction that PMF exists, with founders, investors and employees all unwilling to admit otherwise.
principles.quote: Thus the key stakeholders are all willing participants in an elaborate fiction that the startup has PMF.

principles.text: Being intellectually honest about being pre-PMF increases your odds of reaching PMF.
principles.quote: Not to mention that being intellectually honest about where your startup is in its developmental lifecycle will increase the chances of it becoming a post-PMF company.

principles.text: Shipping a controversial technology is how powerful tech reaches the world; the defector is the vector.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton and PB of Standard Capital explain how wealth is created (positive-sum exchange, marketplaces, better decisions) and why founders should know exactly where their startup creates it. Dalton's advice: make customers far better off than you, and capture only a slice of the value you create.

chunks.heading: Why founders should know where their startup creates wealth
chunks.text:
- Dalton says the reason for the video is to give founders one piece of advice: understand how your startup creates wealth.
- The more wealth you create for your users and customers, the better.
- He says that if a founder has no good answer to "where is the wealth created?", "I think that's a problem."

chunks.heading: Positive-sum vs. zero-sum thinking
chunks.text:
- He argues that people who distrust startups are not so different from investors. Both sort companies into a "positive-sum, creates wealth" bucket and a "scam" bucket.
- He says the anti-tech view puts everything in the bad bucket, so Google, Gmail and everything Standard Capital funds count as ripping people off. He clearly does not hold that view.
- He treats this as a difference in criteria for who creates wealth, not a difference in whether wealth creation matters.

chunks.heading: Marketplaces as examples of positive-sum value
chunks.text:
- Dalton points to eBay as an original dot-com-era startup. As he tells it, the Beanie Babies maker was so badly run that it shipped certain Beanie Babies to only some parts of the US. eBay let people with a glut of one type sell to buyers elsewhere, so "everyone was better off."
