- He cites Whatnot, "one of my best investments at YC," as a modern eBay competitor. Many people make a living selling on its live streams, and "it certainly seems positive sum to me."

chunks.heading: Value delivered vs. value captured
chunks.text:
- Dalton's test for whether a startup makes wealth is to compare how much value its customers get with how much the startup itself captures.
- His example is Google. Users get far more value from it than Google captures, such as businesses getting customers and people researching a company. Standard Capital gets value because people searching for various terms end up on its website.
- He says "the actual value that's being captured by the corporation is a tiny fraction of how much their users are being benefited."
- His one-line conclusion for founders is to create more value than you capture, and to have a clear idea of where your startup creates wealth.

chunks.heading: Being much better, not slightly cheaper
chunks.text:
- Dalton says you create value not by being the lowest-cost option, but by being "so much better than other options."
- He says "trying to be slightly cheaper than someone else is not creating value."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton Caldwell and PB (Standard Capital) explain what separates good from bad angel investors. Bad ones fear loss, slow-walk diligence, try to control founders and often have no real budget; good ones move fast, diversify and accept most bets go to zero. Includes concrete screening questions for founders.

chunks.heading: Why "all investors are the same" is a founder's naive mistake
chunks.text:
- Dalton says that as a first-time founder he assumed investors were interchangeable: "people that give you money." You talk, they wire, you move on.
- He only understood the gap between good and bad investors after being a founder for a long time.
- His view is that the investing process itself differs hugely between a good and a bad investor, and the gap is largest at the extremes.
- The advice is aimed at angel and pre-seed investing. Dalton notes that losing everything on a deal is the normal outcome there. It is the opposite of stocks or real estate, where going to zero means something went badly wrong.

chunks.heading: A good investor's process is simple, and sophistication shows in it
chunks.text:
- Dalton says a great process is a sign of a sophisticated investor.
- The least experienced angels often come from real estate or public-market investing. He calls their approach "super midwit" process:
  - Meet us three times.
  - Have four people on the call.
  - Send three-year financial projections.
- Asking all this of a two-person startup is "silly crap," in his words.
- He finds it telling that people with no angel experience are the ones full of bad ideas about how to run a process.

chunks.heading: Investors with no real money, or a tiny budget
chunks.text:
- Some "investors" simply have no money.
  - Their plan is to get a startup to accept their terms, then raise the money from someone else and act as a middleman between capital and the startup.
  - Dalton calls this classic bad behavior.
- Others have a tiny budget but still take hundreds of founder meetings to make one investment.
- A good investor decides how much they will devote to startups and then invests it. Making a decision and moving on is straightforward for them.
- Dalton agrees that "not caring as much" about the individual dollars is a good thing.

chunks.heading: The screening test: ask about recent investments
chunks.text:
- When founders ask how to tell a good angel or pre-seed investor from a bad one, Dalton gives this concrete test. Ask:
  - How many other investments have you made in the past year?
  - How big were the checks?
  - Which companies were they?
- Then contact those founders and ask whether this person really invested in them.
- He thinks this simple check screens out about 80% of bad investors.
- Green flags: roughly 20 deals in the past year, similar check sizes, and founders who say "they're cool."
- Red flag: he feels bad for founders who spend months and months with investors who, in truth, haven't invested in anyone in the last year. The whole thing is a waste of time.

chunks.heading: Check size and number of bets
chunks.text:
- Dalton recounts a party conversation with a doctor who wanted angel investing tips. The doctor planned to put his money into one large investment in a single company.
- Dalton suggested splitting it into about 10 much smaller checks. He explained portfolio theory and the expected value logic, and says the doctor was convinced.
- His framing is that you get to roll the dice, and he calls 10 rolls "way better" than one.
  - Putting everything on one roll reduces nothing about the upside if you hit.
  - Ten rolls lowers the upside slightly but raises the odds that you hit a very good investment.
  - He suggests running a Monte Carlo simulation, or asking ChatGPT, to see this.

chunks.heading: Inexperienced investors become a constant source of problems after you take their money
chunks.text:
- Dalton says the unsophisticated or inexperienced ones "suck up a lot of time" once they are on your cap table.
- Examples of what they send founders:
  - An email every week saying they read an article and are really worried.
  - Intros to totally random people, such as "my neighbor knows about computers."
- In his words, they become a "vector for annoying junk."

chunks.heading: Slow processes are a bad sign at every stage
chunks.text:
- For pre-seed, he says to ask questions that test how sophisticated an investor is, and how many investments they have made.
- At later stages the same logic holds: an "inappropriately prolonged process" is a bad sign.
  - His examples are a six-month or a three-month fundraise process.
  - He says he doesn't know anyone good who does that.
  - If a founder tolerates it, they are selecting for bad investors.
- On returns, Dalton's argument is that the slowest investors have the worst returns.
  - No good founder would tolerate a very slow process. They would talk to someone with a faster one.
  - That creates selection bias. The struggling startups with the hardest fundraises are the only ones who put up with slow investors, so they end up with the saddest stories.
- From his time as a YC partner: his strongest companies said fundraising was "pretty straightforward." The insane stories, which he says he could never repeat on video, came from companies having a hard raise.
- His conclusion is that there is a market matching effect, and "you don't want to be on the bottom part of the market."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton Caldwell and PB discuss how feeds and LLMs can distort a founder's thinking, drawing on Dalton's FriendFeed experience creating the like button. The fix is limits, gaps away from screens, and grounding in real people and real customers who say no to your product.

chunks.heading: Info hazards are mostly about getting sucked in, and the fix is staying grounded
chunks.text: Dalton's view on this topic is only partly recoverable from this transcript: PB does most of the talking on feeds, the like button and the "jar of sand" analogy, so those are left out. What follows are the points that clearly come from Dalton.

chunks.heading: Media history: shared TV, cable bubbles, and online communities
chunks.text:
- Dalton frames the history of info hazards as: television, then cable, then online communities, then social feeds, then LLMs.
- Early TV had two or three channels. His view is that there was not much info hazard then, because everyone consumed the same content. He jokes that "everyone got brainwashed the same."
- Cable created filter bubbles. A kid in the US watching Nickelodeon, Comedy Central and MTV shared more culture with a kid a thousand miles away watching the same channels than with neighbors watching different ones. He grew up on Nickelodeon, Comedy Central and music-video-era MTV, and says it affected his state of mind.
- His mother was afraid of this, so his house had no cable.
- Online forums let you find people just like you, which is great. But you can fool yourself into thinking niche or fringe opinions are widely held when everyone in your forum agrees. He notes that if you're watching this video, you're probably in a YouTube filter bubble that recommended it.

chunks.heading: Social media: it isn't real life, and it feeds you more of what you click
chunks.text:
- Dalton still uses x.com and says he has an "okay relationship" with it and isn't overly addicted.
- His core reminder: it's not real life. You can close the window and almost nothing that happens there matters (an earthquake would be the exception).
- He tells his kids that Instagram feels real and kind of isn't. His advice is to remind yourself over and over that entertaining content is fine, but it isn't your actual life.
- Viral content skews negative. His view is that the biggest ramification of staying in feeds too long is that you get depressed, and the usual fix is to "close the window and go exercise."

chunks.heading: Immune systems for new media
chunks.text:
- Dalton's mental model: when a new form of social media appears, people have no immune system, like a new virus where everyone catches it. Young people who grew up with it develop better natural immunity.
- Example: boomers on Facebook believing AI slop, versus young people who are much better at spotting it.
- On LLMs, he says we don't yet have an immune system. Nobody has defined a healthy amount of usage, and there are many shades of gray between a power user and "AI psychosis."
- Is it appropriate to ask an LLM about every micro-decision in your life? He says the jury is out.

chunks.heading: LLM filter bubbles and validation
chunks.text:
- Dalton warns about the model training incentive: you train models to get a thumbs up from the user, so they affirm you. There is a fine line between wanting to talk to the model all the time and unhealthy dependence.
- His advice: be especially wary of an LLM validating big life decisions, or fantastical claims about your abilities that aren't backed by reality.
- He notes LLMs have created a new class of crackpots who believe they've solved physics.
- **Never use these tools as a mirror of yourself.** People get in trouble when they judge who they are by the reflection technology gives back, e.g. asking Claude "Who am I? Do you understand me? My friends don't get me." His reaction: "Don't do that, man."
- Have a firm idea of who you are outside of these things.

chunks.heading: The positive case: these tools make you smarter, if you can disconnect
chunks.text:
- Dalton is convinced YouTube made him smarter because he watches videos that teach him things.
- He says TikTok made him smarter too. He learned about exercise, personal health, running and swimming tips, and music theory. In a parallel universe without TikTok, he thinks he'd know much less about all of it.
- The downside is spending all day on it until you "couldn't hold down a job."
- Same for LLMs: they're already making him smarter (e.g. posting a photo of something and asking questions). The test is whether they fill a crippling place in your life. His benchmark: "I can function without talking to Claude every 20 minutes."
- Practical tests and habits: can you disconnect, and can you stay away over the weekend.
- Go outdoors without earbuds. You don't have to listen to podcasts all the time either. Just walk or run.

chunks.heading: Staying grounded: in-person peers and real customers
chunks.text:
- Dalton's keyword is "grounded." Staying grounded in physical reality comes from real people you know, from going outdoors, and from customers.
- Standard Capital focuses on in-person time. Its group office hours format forces founders to come in person, away from screens.
- He values real peers you know in real life, plus a Slack channel with all the founders, over only having X followers. If all the startup people you know are anonymous accounts with anime profile pictures, "you could get in a pretty weird spot."
- On customers: as a founder you can convince yourself everyone wants your product. But "when you ask people for money, they say no." He calls actually trying to sell a product a form of grounding. Claude will tell you your idea for a french fry salad is awesome, but when you try to sell it you find out for real.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton and PB of Standard Capital share what founders should do right after a Series A. Hire gradually into roles you understand, set a hard 12-month goal, spend only into proven channels and bank the rest, and treat the round as a starting line, not a finish line.

chunks.heading: What Dalton wants founders to do after a Series A
chunks.text:
Dalton frames the Series A as a starting line, not a finish line. His definition: raise it when you have product-market fit. From that point the job is to scale, grow and hire, but carefully.

- "Congratulations, you won the prize. Your award is more work."
- He compares it to getting into YC: founders expect easy street, and instead it "was like, oh, no, this is really hard." He says he levels with founders that it is only the beginning of the pain.
- The practical takeaway is to treat the round as an arbitrary checkpoint. Take it in stride, use the money and resources to reach the next level, and enjoy hard things. The game only gets harder from here.

chunks.heading: Hiring after the Series A: where it helps and where it hurts
chunks.text:
Dalton's view is that hiring should accelerate something that already works.

- **Seed vs. Series A.** He does not give seed companies the same hiring advice. At seed, you may still pivot, and hiring can accelerate you in the wrong direction. At Series A, you are hopefully already moving in the right direction, so hiring helps you move faster.
- **Sales and engineering.** The typical Series A hires are salespeople (the founder has already sold successfully) and engineers added to an existing team. The aim is "adding more fuel to the fire."
- **Anti-pattern 1: hiring too fast.** He uses a rowboat image. One person climbing in won't tip it, but ten jumping in at once will. Going from 5 people to 20 can wreck culture, so ease hires in gradually.
- **Anti-pattern 2: under-hiring.** Some founders have read too many tweets about building a "decacorn with no employees." His answer: "Seems like Anthropic and OpenAI are still hiring... check back in with me when Anthropic stops hiring people."
- The goal is not to avoid hiring. The goal is to build a great company.
- **Compensation.** Startups often pay under market before the A and promise employees that things improve after it. At the A stage, it is appropriate to move closer to market pay.

chunks.heading: Founders should do the job first, then hire someone to replace themselves
chunks.text:
This is a core rule at Standard Capital.

- Hire into roles where you already know how the work is done. A common failure is a founder dropping someone whose whole career was at a big company into a startup as, say, VP of sales, when the founder has never done sales.
- If you have done the job successfully and the new hire is failing, you can coach them or let them go. If you have never done it, you cannot tell whether the job is simply hard.
- This is why Dalton wants at least one technical founder. It is easy for engineers to "snow" non-technical people, and you cannot manage what you do not understand.
- His advice: understand every level of your startup and be able to do the work at every level, because debugging is far easier when you do.

chunks.heading: Setting 6, 12 and 18 month goals after the A
chunks.text:
After investing at the Series A, Standard Capital asks each company for 6-month, 12-month and 18-month goals.

- Dalton's main point: "To me, the most important thing is just having the goal." For many founders the goal was to get to the Series A, so afterward the question is "okay, you made it. Now what?"
- A typical 12-month goal for portfolio companies is going from roughly $2M ARR to $10M. He calls $10M "the magic number."
- Helping founders visualize what it takes to reach $10M means asking which tactics can actually get there. He notes it is hard to reach $10M ARR buying Facebook ads, and that some seed-stage tactics will not carry you through.
- Goals should be ambitious but achievable. You should be able to work backward from the goal to today and name the steps along the way.
- He says the mistake of slowing down after raising is "exactly wrong."

chunks.heading: Runway and burn: spend only when you have a channel that pays back
chunks.text:
Dalton's position is that it depends, but with a clear test.

- **If you have a very effective growth channel you can spend into, spend aggressively.** His example: a startup finds that salespeople each carry a quota and pay for themselves in about six months. In that case, do it a lot, don't be shy about runway, and keep tracking that it works.
- **If you don't have such a channel, it is often smart to bank the money** rather than burn much of it yet.
- He recalls a YC company whose advice to the batch was "only burn the prior round": when you raise a seed, burn your pre-seed; when you raise an A, burn your seed. You then always have the last round in the bank, which means you always have leverage.
- He concedes this is not universal. Hard-tech companies "kind of got to burn the money," and some great companies have come within weeks of running out.
- The real question is "what are you getting for the burn?" Bringing in high-value customers is good burn. He has been disappointed by investments that incinerated money with nothing to show for it.

chunks.heading: Why Dalton, as an investor, tells founders not to burn everything fast
chunks.text:
Dalton describes a pattern he saw as a seed investor and YC partner.

- He often heard that a founder's Series A or B board member pushed them to burn all the money within a year. He allows that this may have been garbled in retelling, or that those investors had reasons he did not know.
- His worry was about alignment. The investor's incentive can be that the company either works, raises the next round and gets a markup, or dies fast so they can leave the board and make another investment. The founder has their whole livelihood in it, and the investor has no skin in that game.
- As a YC partner he found himself disagreeing with later-stage investors' advice and telling founders: "Maybe don't do that... only start burning once you really know it works."
- He tells founders directly that he is an investor and does not want them to burn all the money. Standard Capital is banking on the long-term success of the company.
- He says this was easier to reason about in the era of physical hardware: Google raised to buy servers, the servers earned ad revenue, and that funded more servers. Once everything became software, it felt easier to lose sight of where the money goes.

chunks.heading: Avoid building a startup on the greater fool theory
chunks.text:
Dalton's rule: "Never run a startup that is implicitly betting on the greater fool theory."

- Flip the assumption. Your most foolish investors should be your earliest ones, and each later round should be smarter. If your late-stage investors look like geniuses, you are on the right track.
- His test for founders is to imagine a smarter person investing in the next round. That person is unlikely to be excited by "we blew all the money on the Super Bowl ad." They would respond to "we bought really valuable assets" or "we did something very effective with the money."
- The alternative is "just hoping there's some other schmuck that will continue to invest in the company."
- **Theranos.** He notes most Silicon Valley investors steered clear because when asked how it worked, the answer was "it's secret." The backers were people sophisticated in politics, not in investing in technology companies. He also recalls privately describing another company years earlier as "Theranos, but real," and that company turned out to be fraudulent too.
- **Fake graphs.** He agrees that selling a dollar for 50 cents makes growth easy, and that you can produce those charts without having a real business. He links this to the Uber-era habit of investors pressing startups to burn faster.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton and Paul of Standard Capital explain why public-market revenue multiples set the ceiling for startup valuations. Key warning: AI-enabled service companies get valued like the legacy service firms they disrupt unless founders prove a technology-sized, growing market.

chunks.heading: Revenue multiples are driven by expected future cash flows, not current revenue
chunks.text:
Dalton explains that valuation comes from discounted cash flows: what a company will earn in 5, 10 and 15 years, not just today.
- A business with strong cash today but a declining market deserves a low multiple, because its future cash flows are low.
- A high-growth company with little profit today can deserve a high multiple if it is believed to become hugely valuable.
- He frames the practical question for a founder as: how much money will this business make in 10 or 20 years?

chunks.heading: Why startups should care about public-market multiples
chunks.text:
Dalton says everyone in startup land is affected by the stock market, even if public prices feel far away.
- Public companies in a startup's category are the comparables it gets valued against.
- Right now many SaaS companies trade at very low revenue multiples. He says this hurts SaaS startups through a "downwind effect" on their valuations.
- The opposite held in the 2021 stock market bubble, when high public multiples led startups to raise at very high valuations.
- Public companies show the spread: one may trade at 1x revenue and another at a thousand times revenue.

chunks.heading: The Tesla lesson: valuing a market, not a product
chunks.text:
Dalton uses Tesla to show why multiples diverge.
- Viewed only as a car company, it should trade like one. Car companies get low multiples because they face competition, have limited margins, and are not expected to grow 10x. GM will not sell 100 times as many cars.
- For a long time Tesla was worth more than every other car company combined, which drove many experienced short sellers "crazy".
- He argues the market may have been rational. The upside is autonomy (robotaxis) and humanoid robots for labor replacement, a market he calls effectively unlimited in size.
- The stock acts like a call option on those outcomes. If Tesla were only a niche car maker, he says it would be a terrible investment.

chunks.heading: AI-enabled services companies: why they get valued like the business they replace
chunks.text:
Dalton flags a risk in the hot new startup category: AI-native versions of traditional service businesses, such as an AI-native law firm that looks like a law firm to the customer but uses AI models underneath.
- Legacy service companies trade at low multiples of revenue or cash flow, perhaps 1x or 2x depending on the business.
- At a 2x multiple, a company with $1 million in annual revenue is worth $2 million.
- Founders must be aware of this and bring proof points and a story for why they should be valued as a technology company with technology multiples, not as the service company they are disrupting.

chunks.heading: Finite market versus infinite market
chunks.text:
Dalton's core test for whether a startup deserves a high multiple is whether it is growing into a finite or an unlimited market.
- A market that is flat or shrinking is unexciting for investors. A market that may be 10x or 100x larger in future has unlimited growth potential.
- Dentistry example: great products exist, but he would not expect dental spend to grow 10x in 10 years.
- Security example: AI makes securing systems more urgent, so he can imagine security growing 10x in 10 years, which is a far more exciting market.
- Healthcare: fighting over a fixed pie, such as squeezing money from insurance claims, is a capped game. Creating something new, like longevity, taps near-infinite budget because people will pay almost anything to live longer with higher quality of life.
- Advice to founders: ask how your market grows and whether AI and related trends will make it larger or smaller. If it is shrinking, consider a new direction.

chunks.heading: SpaceX: turning a finite market into an infinite one
chunks.text:
Dalton uses SpaceX to show how a founder can change the market-size answer.
- Early on, people were bearish because the global launch market was small, and that was true.
- Elon fixed this by creating his own demand with Starlink, which gives him a reason to launch rockets over and over. Dalton says the majority of satellites in space are now SpaceX satellites.
- The market became effectively everything off Earth, including data centers in space, and only SpaceX has the rockets.
- By contrast, he says you would never want to invest in ULA (the traditional launch business) at a high multiple, since it is a fixed-size business now being destroyed.
- He notes it did not "hit people over the head" at first. Many said SpaceX was not different, so it takes creative insight to articulate the difference.

chunks.heading: Practical checklist for founders raising money
chunks.text:
- Look at the big players in your space and ask whether any are worth $100 billion or $200 billion. If the incumbents you hope to displace are worth single-digit billions, that is a red flag, and you must explain why you will be worth 100x as much.
- Ask ChatGPT for the comparables of your company and see how they are valued. He notes that for many startups the comps that come up are a company just acquired by private equity for about $400 million, or a very small-cap company. That may sound like a lot but "that's not great".
- Do this research on comparables and how they are valued before you pitch.
- If the comps are not great, build a really good story for why you will be worth far more than them.
- Revenue alone does not decide the outcome. Standard Capital sometimes passes on a company with $5 million of revenue and funds one with almost none, because market size and growth matter more.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton and PB from Standard Capital discuss which startups the AI labs will run over. Dalton's points: don't build workarounds for today's model flaws, hard-to-build software is no longer a moat, and the internet era shows who adapts and who gets crushed.

chunks.heading: "What if Google does this?" and the turkey-graph risk
chunks.text:
- Dalton recalls being a founder and rolling his eyes when investors asked "Oh, what if Google does this?" He calls it the cop-out question every investor asks, and admits this line of thinking can annoy founders.
- He argues AI changes the answer: models keep getting smarter and faster, so some startups are implicitly betting the models won't improve.
- He asks whether a founder's business is "turkey graph" shaped: customers and revenue look great until a lab moves into the space.

chunks.heading: Building around model weaknesses is a short bet on the model
chunks.text:
- Dalton's example: building "bread middleware" to make models work in use cases where they're deficient. In his words, that is "the definition of a turkey startup", because a new model drops and it's game over.
- His analogy: building "googledogs.com" because Google Search is bad at searching for kinds of dogs. That is a bet that Google won't get better.
- He summarizes it as making a short bet on the model provider, and calls that a bad bet.
- He frames the diagnostic question for founders: how do you know whether you're exposed or can feel okay?

chunks.heading: Which businesses are safest
chunks.text:
- Dalton asks which businesses are safest from the labs and from clones, and who needs to worry least.
- He asks what a founder should do who is early enough to pivot.
- He asks what a larger company should do, using the example of a Series B SaaS company. When told "panic", he pushes: "You got to do more than that."

chunks.heading: The internet as the best comparison for AI
chunks.text:
- Dalton calls the internet his best comp. He allows that AI may be bigger than the internet, "we'll see".
- Incumbents hit by the internet were slow to react. His examples are Barnes & Noble and Blockbuster, which faced internet-native competitors.
- Others adapted and survived. His example is the big banks (Bank of America, Wells Fargo), which stayed okay despite online banking changing their business.
- He asks which categories were totally hosed by the internet, offering music stores as a first guess.
- He concludes that businesses selling media had no move other than pivoting into a different line of business.

chunks.heading: Pure software moats
chunks.text:
- Dalton's conclusion: pure software businesses whose moat is "that it's hard to build" will have a bad time.
- He also asks which businesses did fine when the internet arrived. Car companies are the example in the discussion, where the internet's distribution effects didn't touch them.

chunks.heading: Energy and compute as the bottleneck
chunks.text:
- Dalton argues the bottleneck to doing interesting things is energy. Early computers were limited by processing power and RAM.
- His example: Bill Gates and his peers were trying to do almost impossible things by laying out every single byte. Nobody worries about that now.
- As energy and compute become more abundant, the scale of what you can do easily gets bigger. He says this runs all the way to colonizing space and building worlds on Mars.
- He asks the discussion to paint a picture of limitless free energy, and ends on "I like that" when the "every problem is a physics problem" framing comes up.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton Caldwell and PB look back on funding hard tech at YC (Ginkgo, Rigetti, Helion, OpenAI) and how it shapes Standard Capital. Back real builders with big ambition, expect less competition on outrageous ideas, and finance hard tech in stages by performing miracles rather than raising everything at once.

chunks.heading: Hard tech at YC was widely ridiculed at the time
chunks.text:
- Dalton frames the topic as what he and PB learned funding hard tech companies at YC "way before that was a thing". The first one he recalls Sam recruiting was Ginkgo Bioworks.
- He describes the reaction to the early hard tech batches as ridicule on all sides.
- Investors asked what "YC bozos" know about hard problems. Sam was "the guy from Loopt", YC had "the Gmail guy", and he quotes the line "what does Paul Graham know, he was like an artist".
- Investors also mocked the founders for taking "such bad terms": a big ownership stake for a small amount of money, with no board seat.
- The wider market thought "none of this stuff is ever going to work". In biotech, companies that chose YC were ridiculed by their peers.
- Dalton says he could never have imagined how many of these companies would succeed. He calls the hit rate "incredible".

chunks.heading: Why hard tech worked: few qualified founders act as a moat
chunks.text:
- Dalton finds it counterintuitive that hard ideas had such a high hit rate. In a typical software idea space, 100 people work on the same thing or pivot into it.
- A quantum computer company is different, because very few people are qualified to build one.
- His example is Chad Rigetti's demo day slide. It was a Venn diagram: the set of people qualified to start a quantum computer company, and the set who want to. Chad was the intersection, "cuz it was such an academic field".
- His conclusion: "there were so few people that could start companies like that that it inadvertently was a moat."
- On space, he says to take out the cranks and count only real attempts at space launch. Twenty years ago it "was just pure insanity", though it is cool now.

chunks.heading: Raise capital in stages, with each stage proving a "miracle"
chunks.text:
- Dalton's first tidbit for hard tech founders: "financing risk is real".
- Software companies usually raise on revenue, growth and momentum. Hard tech companies have none of those.
- Their milestones are therefore "what miracles you performed". The founder has to keep performing miracles and choose the right ones to argue they have made enough progress to raise again.
- This requires a sophisticated view of how much capital is needed to reach the next miracle.
- The intuitive approach is wrong. Many founders think they can say "I want to build a lunar moon base, let's put up a hotel, give me a billion dollars", and he stresses "that is not how it works".
- Instead, separate each stage of capital and decide what that raise will prove. He says YC saw this "over and over again" with its companies.
- His advice on investors: don't expect them to see the brilliance of the idea and fund the end state at once. Keep setting yourself up to succeed by doing amazing things, and raise at each stage to reach the next level.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ex-YC partner Dalton Caldwell walks through classic YC advice (pick a non-obvious idea, build a simple MVP, talk to users, raise less, win by being unignorable) and how each updates with AI coding tools. Core theme: AI makes features and code cheap, so focus, direct user conversations and unconventional ideas matter more, not less.

chunks.heading: Why there is "no secret" in YC advice
chunks.text:
- Dalton says "the secret is there is no secret." Office hours test a founder's own thinking, like a coach who sharpens a craft the founder already has, rather than handing over hidden knowledge.
- The big trap is the "midwit" end of the bell curve. Founders overthink and stress instead of taking the simplest approach.
- The core advice still holds, but the details need updating as the ideas change. Early YC ideas were mostly web versions of desktop software, and today's are different.

chunks.heading: Why startup ideas have gotten narrower
chunks.text:
- Early YC had no content machine about startups. Paul Graham's blog took off because nothing like it existed, and Dalton read Marc Andreessen's pmarca blog as a founder.
- In the 2000s, founders mostly picked ideas that resembled VC-funded ones, ideas advisors endorsed, or totally zany ones. He recalls a YC applicant with a truck that baked muffins on the way to deliver them fresh.
- Today so much startup content exists that the "aperture" of conceivable ideas is smaller. This raises the floor, because the worst ideas disappear, but it also screens out truly unusual ones.
- He says OpenAI would have been very hard to pitch the year it started, since it was a research project and not a business.
- He cites space and nuclear companies as ideas that were hard to explain a decade ago and are now legible. Fintech was also outside the aperture: banks wouldn't partner, and Bank Simple took about 3 years to launch a prepaid debit card and sold for roughly $100 million.
- The best time to invest in an idea is before it fits the aperture. Investors told him fintech was a warning story.

chunks.heading: Favor weird, obsessive, non-conformist founders
chunks.text:
- Unconventional people tend to be unconventional in everything, including their ideas. His examples are Marc Andreessen, Paul Graham and Elon Musk.
- When he met Elon around 2008, Elon talked at him for 2 hours about SpaceX before it existed. Elon's opening line was "my plan is to die on Mars, hopefully not on impact."
- Career-optimizing "leveling up" types (valedictorian, elite college, MBA, fancy job) are very smart but struggle most at ideation, because everything they've done sits inside the aperture.
- Wanting recognition and praise makes it hard to come up with a truly weird idea.

chunks.heading: Pivot early and pick ideas by unfair advantage
chunks.text:
- He encourages pivoting during YC: "If you're going to spend the next decade of your life on something and you're not 100% sure you're working on the right idea, it's much easier to fix it today than tomorrow." Pivoting inside a batch costs nothing, and 5 years in it is brutal.
- Founders often ask for a list of ideas. His method is to start from the founder's unfair advantages, find areas of context and advantage, and apply them to the emerging technology.
- Obvious ideas built on a new platform rarely win big. The cloud era made a CRUD app easy for everyone to build, and the iPhone App Store era rewarded Uber and DoorDash more than the obvious apps.
- For AI, the most obvious ideas, with thousands of startups doing the same thing, are unlikely to yield big outcomes. The winners will use AI to do something that wasn't possible before.
- Anyone can write code with AI, and "that is not enough." It has to combine with something inspired that delivers real value to users.

chunks.heading: Build the MVP: one clear feature, not many
chunks.text:
- Paul Graham's advice to use AWS instead of racking servers sped up YC startups. Dropbox was derided as a thin wrapper on AWS, and the cloud was a competitive edge against slow legacy companies.
- "Do things that don't scale" originally meant skipping scalability work and building the pure essence of what delivers value. Google's impressive part was a search engine users loved, not its back end.
- With coding tools, features are cheap, but a product with 80 unfinished or half-finished features won't get adopted, and you may never get a second shot. A low-quality product is hard to fix by adding features.
- Examples of starting simple and widening: PostHog started with product analytics, then added rings around it. Robinhood started with free stock trading, and Coinbase with buying Bitcoin in a non-sketchy way.
- To compete with Robinhood, he would not clone its features. He would pick one distinctive feature people can explain and add more around it later.
- Customers should be able to explain back what the product is and why they want it.

chunks.heading: Launch now and build in public
chunks.text:
- Most founders overestimate how much people care about their startup. Talking about what you're building is a form of marketing and community-building, and for developer tools, posting on Twitter or Hacker News is how you get early customers.
- "Most startups die not because someone copied your idea, it's just because no one ever heard that you existed."
- Posting a lot creates luck. Open source and network-effect businesses have little to fear from copying, though some easily clonable businesses might stay quiet.
- In his portfolio, he can think of only one company that doesn't want to talk much. Even then, some public presence helps recruit engineers, since a no-footprint startup with non-famous founders is hard to hire for.
- A secrecy-dependent idea worries him, because "eventually you're going to be attacked by the clone army."

chunks.heading: Talk to users, especially now
chunks.text:
- Paul Graham's advice was counterintuitive in the 2000s because founders built websites and used viral flows, SEO and ad buys. Talking to users one at a time seemed unscalable, like digging a hole with a spoon when an excavator is available.
- Talking in person gives context a dashboard doesn't: nuance, body language and what users are doing.
- It's now easier to hide behind the keyboard with ads, viral loops, paid influencers and AI agents that deliver reports. That loses the nuance, so talking to users matters more.
- "Sitting down and talking to 20 or 30 people is going to give you more information about if you're on the right track than signing up 10,000 randos from Google Ads." Scale ads and viral flows later, once things are dialed in on small numbers.
- Example: his co-founder Paul built Gmail first for himself, then sat with users at the Google office until he had 100 happy users, asking what features to add next.
- Talking to users keeps the humanity in view and gives the product soul. Products built by someone who never talked to users feel like features glued together. He cites Gusto as a boring product with soul.

chunks.heading: Fundraising and selling the company
chunks.text:
- Fundraising has become a status game (amount, valuation, investors) because it's legible to parents and LinkedIn. Some founders love it, others find it awkward, and YC was built for the latter by putting the process on rails.
- Pre-seed: less is better because constraints force focus. Giving a pre-idea company $5M leads to hiring and feature sprawl that doesn't help build an MVP. YC invests half a million dollars, which he calls enough for a two-person startup for 2 years with no revenue.
- Raise more only with a hard constraint, such as an AI training run, FDA approval or a banking license. Investors "neg" founders with "you want to be ambitious, right?", which he calls an effective trick.
- Seed rule of thumb in YC: stay below 15% dilution. Raising a few million for 10-15% is "a pretty good trade," and the band to avoid is something like 20 on 40.
- His new firm, Standard Capital (a Series A fund), copies the YC process:
  - Application on the website with no warm intro, and founders state their own valuation.
  - 10% dilution rounds at Series A.
  - No board seat, as with PG at YC.
  - Group office hours, an idea Paul invented. Founders learn more from respected peers doing the same thing than from a professional investor at board meetings. Groups are reshuffled yearly by traction, so the highest-traction companies end up together.
- Selling the company: the best way is to grow so fast you destroy competitors, who then want to buy you. Examples: Google bought YouTube because it was beating Google Video, and Facebook bought Instagram because it was a frightening threat. Time spent networking with corp dev doesn't help.
- If you're that successful you probably don't want to sell, like Facebook. "Be so successful that you don't need to be acquired."

chunks.heading: Hiring, and sleep and exercise
chunks.text:
- Hiring: Anthropic keeps hiring engineers, so there is still incremental value in hiring across sales, marketing, growth and engineering. Dalton says to revisit when the labs stop hiring engineers.
- Middle management seems to be shrinking, because its main job of tracking work and synthesizing reports can now be done with AI.
- Sleep and exercise: burnout kills many startups, and it may be a bigger risk now. He has seen founders burn out, and says vibe coding with Claude is so fun that founders stay up all night, feeling the window is closing ("AI psychosis").
- YC opened every batch with a talk on sleep and exercise. He still stands by it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton Caldwell explains that pivoting is just changing your idea and should feel lightweight early on. He covers why founders pivot too late (loss aversion, politeness mistaken for traction), good and bad reasons to pivot, and a four-part scoring rubric for the next idea, illustrated with YC examples like Brex, Retool, Magic and Segment.

chunks.heading: Pivoting is part of the earliest stage of a startup
chunks.text:
- Dalton defines a pivot as simply changing your idea. Strictly, a "true" pivot is a real company with users and funding shutting down one product to build another. His example is Slack, which had raised money and had about 100 employees on the video game Glitch before shutting it down.
- He says that pre-launch or just after launch, changing ideas should feel lightweight. "If you're not in a state where you're rapidly changing ideas or assumptions over and over and over again in quick succession, you are likely doing it wrong. You are likely moving too slow."
- He argues most founders take too long to pivot, not too short.
- He says founders should own the decision. They should not ask a YC partner or other authority figure to tell them when to give up. "It's your life and if it works out good or bad, that's on you." Advisors can only give guidance.

chunks.heading: Why pivot: opportunity cost and more shots on goal
chunks.text:
- Dalton's main reason to pivot is opportunity cost: you can only really work on one thing at a time, so working on something with evidence it isn't working costs you the chance to work on something else.
- He wrote a joke formula: (how well things are working ÷ months of concerted full-time effort). If that is lower than (excitement to work on something else + confidence you can find something better), pivot. The driver is months spent without it working.
- Months of effort matter. A couple of weeks in, the signal is weak. Many months with nothing is a strong signal.
- Pivoting gives more shots on goal at product market fit. Dalton says most people never get PMF. You know you have it "when growth is not your biggest problem. It's other stuff."
- He says it is much easier to be lucky with half a dozen shots than one, so multiple shots "create luck for yourself". The shots must be high quality: make something, complete it, ship it, and get it to people. Pivoting through ideas without really launching them doesn't count.

chunks.heading: Good and bad reasons to pivot
chunks.text:
Good reasons:
- You hate working on it.
- It isn't growing and nothing is happening.
- You are not a good fit for the idea.
- You depend on an external factor you don't control, such as mainstream VR headset adoption or mainstream crypto adoption.
- You are out of ideas on how to make it work.
- You know in your heart it isn't working. Dalton says many founders secretly know and keep up a front. "You know more than anyone else about your business."
- The idea is impossible to start, such as "once we raise $100 million, then we will build a prototype".
- You have launched and spent weeks or months trying to get users and it feels hopeless.

Bad reasons:
- Running away from hard work. Some founders build a product and pivot right when it is time to sell, repeatedly.
- Being a chronic idea-changer. He recommends following something through all the way.
- Chasing a hot new thing because of a TechCrunch article or someone else's funding round.

chunks.heading: Why founders take too long to pivot
chunks.text:
- Loss aversion: once you have invested, it is hard to let go.
- A little traction, such as a few users or one customer, makes you think "maybe it'll work".
- Politeness mistaken for traction. People rarely say they will never be a customer. They say "this is great, add a few more features and come back." Founders can loop on this for years without getting customers.
- Fear of admitting weakness or defeat.
- Blaming customers or investors, with the belief that "the world is wrong" and the idea is ahead of its time.
- Inspirational messages that say believe hard enough and keep going.

**The "uncanny valley of product market fit":** Dalton noticed at YC that a company whose idea totally fails immediately has a weird advantage over one with a little traction. The first can write off the idea, with no second-guessing, and move on. A little traction can trap talented people for long periods.

**Anecdotes:** He says stories of founders who persisted for 5 years and then won are true but not actionable, like lottery winners. He prefers advice that plays the statistics and takes accountability.

chunks.heading: How to find a better idea to pivot to
chunks.text:
- Pick something you are more excited about, that makes you more optimistic about the world and more excited to wake up and work on.
- A counterintuitive corollary: a perceived harder idea is often better. Boring ideas like ad networks, ad tech and affiliate or ad targeting "never work" because nobody is inspired by them. His example is a batch company that moved from ad tech to a "Robin Hood for India". "The founders lit up" and the excitement was contagious. It was the same founders; the change was a real idea they cared about.
- Make an honest, self-aware assessment of what you are good and bad at, and play to your strengths.
- Choose something you can build and validate very quickly, not a year or two of R&D. Pivoting from one thing that is impossible to ship to another is a bad sign.
- It is fine to build a business that won't raise venture capital, since most businesses don't need it. If you do want VC, the idea matters a lot, and founders get frustrated trying to raise for things that aren't fundable.

**Rules of thumb for VC-fundable ideas** (he says there is no official guidebook):
- You can imagine hundreds of millions or billions in net revenue per year.
- You can imagine getting there in less than 10 years, or 5, and fast.
- You can picture it as a publicly traded company someday.
- Technology is a key component and the founders build it, at least early on.
- High margins, such as 70-80% gross margins.
- He adds that Shark Tank-style businesses are mostly not venture fundable.

chunks.heading: When to pivot, and the cost of pivoting too much
chunks.text:
- Pivot as soon as you have launched and spent weeks or months trying to get users and it feels hopeless, or the idea can't be started without huge capital, or you know in your heart it isn't working.
- Whiplash from pivoting over and over is bad because it makes founders sad and want to quit, which kills the company. Dalton says this is more deadly than working on a mediocre idea you enjoy: "If you're having fun working on a bad idea, you won't give up." If you hate your life working on your startup, you will not succeed. Aim for a happy medium between pivoting daily for six weeks and working on the same idea for five years.
- Avoid having employees while pivoting. It slows you down and makes them sad. Dalton would add people only after the idea is working and you have confidence. Scaling a team while unsure of the idea is not best practice.

chunks.heading: Scoring ideas: Dalton's 1-10 quality score, with YC examples
chunks.text:
He made up a subjective score for the lecture: rate four criteria 1-10 and average them.

1. **How big it seems.** Is it an obvious publicly traded company (a car company, a bank) or at the Subway-franchise or eBay-import end of the spectrum?
2. **Founder-market fit.** 10 means you worked on self-driving cars through undergrad and your career and now start a self-driving car company. 0 means a startup in advanced AI when you don't know how to program.
3. **How easy it is to get started.** Dalton thinks this is undersold. Many good ideas never work because founders can't find a way to start, then someone later has a better way in and wins. Finding an idea that is easy to start is as important as the idea itself.
4. **Early market feedback.** Do people want it immediately and is the sale straightforward, or is it impossible?

**Brex (YC17)** (named in the transcript only as "BS"; the details match the credit card for startups pivot, and the figures below are as Dalton gave them):
- Before: a VR hardware headset for doing work. Big 6/medium-big, founder-market fit 1/10 (fintech software people with no hardware or optics knowledge), ease of start 2 (needed hardware hires, millions of dollars for a prototype, years of manufacturing), market feedback bad because no one wanted it. Overall 2.5/10.
- After: a credit card for startups. Size 10/10 (many public fintech comps like Square and Stripe), founder-market fit 10 (they had built and sold a fintech company in Brazil for about $20-30 million, and could code and ship it themselves), ease of start 3 (launching a credit card is hard, but the fit made it manageable), market feedback 8 (in the batch, people said yes to being customers).
- Result as Dalton states it: raised hundreds of millions and worth billions in two years. He calls it an outlier and "the most epic pivot of all time", with him having a front-row seat.

**Retool (W17):**
- Before: Venmo for the UK. Seemed big, founder-market fit 3, ease of start 7 (already launched with users), market feedback 3 (no one wanted to pay and they lost money on every transaction). Dalton says this was the insidious kind of traction that made it hard to give up.
- After: a tool for building internal tools. Size 10 (he says 80% of software built is for internal consumption), founder-market fit 10 (one founder had built something similar in a college internship), ease of start 10 (built in two weeks and got the first customers), market feedback 5 (interest but people were unsure about trusting a startup, and it did not fly off the shelves).

**Magic (W15):**
- Before: a blood pressure coach app. Size 2, founder-market fit 2 (no health knowledge), ease of start 8 (built quickly and got users quickly), market feedback poor. People were polite and usage was horrible.
- After: built a prototype in a weekend, posted it on Hacker News where it hit number one with about 2,000 upvotes, went viral overnight and got lots of press. They had about five ideas, and Dalton says nobody could have predicted which would capture the imagination. He credits it as a "shots on goal" example and an inadvertent inspiration for chatbot clones. They built a profitable, sustainable company.

**Segment (S11):**
- Before: a classroom feedback tool where students push a button to tell the professor they are confused. Founder-market fit about 5 (they were students), easy to build, and decent feedback with a bunch of schools adopting it. It took years to discard.
- After: the analytics data collection tool. At the time it wasn't obviously a future public company. Founder-market fit was great because they had built so much analytics and were experts. They open sourced it, gave it away for free, and the market begged them to support it. "If the market's begging for something and you don't even think it's good and they have to convince you it's good, that's a pretty good sign." Segment pivoted multiple times, including years after the batch, and is now worth billions.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton Caldwell explains how Standard Capital brings YC-style standardization to Series A: fixed public terms, founder-set price, no board seat. He also covers what stays defensible once AI can clone software, how to spot flash-in-the-pan growth, how to think about dilution at demo day, and what makes a tarpit idea.

chunks.heading: Standard Capital: YC for the Series A
chunks.text:
- Dalton calls Standard Capital "YC for series A", built with co-founder PB (the inventor of group office hours at YC). Fund one is $425 million, started in summer 2026, with 23 Series A deals led so far.
- As a YC partner, helping the best companies graduate to a Series A was a core part of his job. As a founder who raised a Series A twice, he noticed the product had barely changed, while YC had reinvented the seed stage (the SAFE, demo day).
- He copied YC's format for the A:
  - An application, with no warm intros and no coffee meetings.
  - Standardized docs published on the website, like the YC SAFE. He says Standard is the only Series A firm doing this.
  - A fast decision: two meetings (about half an hour each) to a yes, for checks of up to $10 million.
- His rationale: YC alumni already know this process, so it feels intuitive. A YC founder whose only fundraising experience is demo day will find it natural.
- He sees YC culture as self-reinforcing: YC alumni prefer buying from, hiring and raising from YC-culture people. He tells his own companies to pick investors who share that culture.
- He could imagine doing the same at later stages someday. He notes YC alumni already include S&P 500 companies (Airbnb, DoorDash, Reddit), so the culture can scale.

chunks.heading: No board seats, and peer board meetings instead
chunks.text:
- Founders constantly asked him how to raise a Series A without giving a board seat, or how to give the lead no more than 10%. As a YC partner he had to say it wasn't possible, because nobody offered that deal. Standard is built to supply what founders ask for.
- Standard takes no board seat. Instead, founders attend "peer board meetings" once a quarter, in groups of five or six post-PMF Series A companies, modeled on group office hours.
- His logic: "who has better advice on how to run a fast growing AI company than another founder of a fast growing AI company?" Investors mostly sit in other boards' meetings and repeat what they hear, so Standard cuts out the middleman.
- He compares this to Paul Graham's innovation. Every seed investor took a board seat when YC started, and PG was ridiculed for investing without control. Dalton's view is that the best founders don't need to be bossed around.

chunks.heading: Founders name the price; no negotiation
chunks.text:
- At Standard the founder states the valuation and the check size, and Standard is either in or out. If the price looks off, Standard asks the founder to reconsider and come back, so it stays the founder's decision rather than a haggle.
- Why he does it:
  - The worst part of investing was negotiating against founders. At YC he never negotiated: it was a standard deal for about a thousand companies, and he could say everyone got the same terms.
  - His advice to founders raising an A used to be "make up a number", which leads to a counter-offer and invented stories to meet in the middle. He compares it to bartering at a swap meet and says it makes you dislike the person across the table.
  - Professional investors negotiate constantly, while a founder does it once, so the process is stacked against the founder. He cites the story of an investor who halved the price right before closing.
- At YC demo day founders already state a cap and the amount, and investors are in or out. Countering with "half your cap" would be insulting in that ecosystem, and Standard follows the same norm.
- His analogy: negotiating with a car dealer versus buying a Tesla in the app and hitting "buy". Standard is designed for founders who dislike dealing with car dealers. He accepts it isn't the best fit for founders who enjoy negotiating.

chunks.heading: Will AI clone every SaaS company? What he looks for
chunks.text:
- Standard's application asks what prevents AI from replicating what you build and selling it cheaper. It replaced the older question about big companies copying you.
- His position is that LLMs cloning any piece of software, faster and cheaper, is inevitable: "I don't know how you could take the other side of that bet." The old moat of "we built this and it was hard" is gone. His analogy is digital music breaking the legacy music business after Napster, and he says coding agents "break the business model of a lot of SaaS businesses."
- What he wants is founders who can say "you could clone our product and we'd still have a business." Answers that work:
  - Marketplaces and other network effects. You could tell an agent to clone Airbnb.com, but you still wouldn't have the supply.
  - Data network effects.
  - Economies of scale, where the business only works if you own the whole thing or operate at huge scale.
  - Hard tech or hardware components, which can't be cloned.
- He doesn't supply the answer; he wants the founder to impress him. His YC lesson: the best investments were founders much smarter than the partners who just described the future. At DoorDash's batch, the founders laid out the vision (suburbs city by city, food first, then other items, then global) and "all you had to do was listen."
- Tip: don't have an LLM write the answer, since it's less likely to be unique. YC applications are now noticeably longer, and AI-written slop is a signal that someone isn't serious. He treats AI as best for human augmentation, which is why Standard still has humans doing interviews.
- Will AI replace human founders? He says it's hard to see that far ahead. His short-term signal is that Anthropic and OpenAI keep hiring humans: as long as a human's incremental value exceeds their compensation, headcount keeps growing. He would watch for headcount dropping at those labs.

chunks.heading: Flash-in-the-pan revenue versus enduring value
chunks.text:
- Fast early AI revenue that later drops to zero is not new. In the 2000s and 2010s, many YC companies raised money, bought ads to build a big user base, and evaporated when they turned the ads off. Facebook apps were once a whole VC category that disappeared.
- Nothing is rock solid at any stage: OpenAI versus Anthropic, AWS ending up bigger than Amazon's e-commerce business, Nokia and BlackBerry.
- Enduring value comes from durably giving customers more value than you take from them, "forever". The honest test is whether the price you charge is a tiny fraction of the value the customer gets.
- Cohort retention, revenue retention and NPS are angles on the business rather than the end-all, but bad retention means you aren't creating value. Founders often see bad numbers and say "we'll fix it later" or "hire people", and that is how flame-outs happen. He agrees with the "don't fill a leaky bucket" framing.
- On investing, he says the smartest move is to back the best businesses and never sell, as Buffett did. For the top of the power law you should keep riding it. He still holds DoorDash shares from his batch and sold only some.

chunks.heading: Raising at demo day: dilution and PMF
chunks.text:
- Some companies should raise an A at demo day or within six months of it. Examples he cites: Scale AI and Lora raised at demo day, and DoorDash within six months.
- Revenue alone isn't the test. Some batch companies show big headline revenue without real PMF, and they may be better off raising a normal round and letting it bake. His advice would be a nuanced discussion of PMF signals and use of capital.
- A hockey stick is not the same as PMF. Look at the sales cycle and the quality of retention. Some companies have stronger PMF signals with less of a hockey stick.
- Risk of raising an A too early: you get a board member and the "ready for Series A" expectation. If growth slows, the investor is hard on you, and you may need two years in the wilderness to figure out the business with that pressure.
- Dilution math: raising a large seed and then a Series A six months later from a traditional VC can sell 15-20% twice, around 40% in under a year, which he calls "dumb". One company Standard invested in at demo day took 10% from Standard plus some angels, and ended up with its entire seed plus Series A at about 15% dilution.
- Demo day money is hard to turn down, but he says to be sophisticated and give bespoke advice per company rather than "everyone should do their demo day funds this way". Standard accepts applications from companies at demo day, but they're still rare because strong proof of PMF is unusual.

chunks.heading: Tarpit ideas in the AI era
chunks.text:
- Tarpit definition: an idea that seems good and looks like nobody else is doing it, so it feels like an opportunity. The real reason nobody has done it is that many people have tried and it is structurally hard. Founders crawl in and get stuck. He's been in one himself, and he doesn't call it dumb.
- Classic example: apps to find out what your friends are doing so you can coordinate hanging out.
- Current tarpit-ish ideas he sees:
  - Generic "Claw"-type products, like OpenClaw but subtly different. You compete directly with OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, and need a strong distribution story.
  - B2B workflow orchestration and automation tools ("workflow automation for dentists").
- He isn't saying nobody can win in these. His advice is to research who else is in the space and be able to explain why you win, ideally backed by proof, rather than being "the 5,000th company doing it". The bar is higher if you're in a crowded space, compared with something unusual like a space hotel company.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton Caldwell shares patterns from 1,000+ YC startups. Persistence beats cleverness, good pivots move closer to your expertise, tarpit ideas trap founders with false validation, and early founders should talk to customers in person instead of growth-hacking. He also covers why investors say no and the danger of over-delegating early.

chunks.heading: Resilience: the core job is not dying
chunks.text:
- Dalton's mantra is "just don't die. Just keep your startup going." He says it over and over, and founders often tell him it was the most impactful thing he said, more than any clever move.
- He compares it to coaches miked up in the huddle: even elite performers are coached on mundane fundamentals, because being reminded of the basics puts them in the right mindset.
- In YC and non-YC stories alike, the founders rationally should have given up at some point. Airbnb should have shut down three or four times before YC. Keeping going was an irrational act.
- Nearly every founder goes through a near-death moment where "I guess we're done." Even among those who hit truly hard situations, he guesses around 50% keep it going through sheer will, then look like overnight successes.
- The most common cause of death is not running out of money. Founders usually still have some money but are out of ideas, fight with a co-founder, can't agree on what to work on, and quit. He says you can see in their eyes whether they feel they have "one more try" left.

chunks.heading: When to keep going and when it is fine to stop
chunks.text:
- First test: are you still having fun? Do you enjoy your co-founders, your customers and the problem? If yes, lean toward continuing.
- If the startup is badly hurting you and your relationships, or you don't want to work with your co-founder anymore, lean toward stopping.
- Founders who turn things around tend to love their customers and product. Airbnb's founders liked each other and knew their first hosts by name even while it was going badly.
- Shutting down costs little: "no one will remember that you shut down your company in 10 years," as long as you act with integrity. Life is short, and staying in misery only to avoid losing face is a big opportunity cost.
- His life motto: check in with yourself that you're having fun and value what you spend time on, and if not, change something. As a founder you are in control and can change your own company.

chunks.heading: Pivoting: how to tell when, and what makes a good pivot
chunks.text:
- When to pivot: count how many more ideas you have for making it grow. With a dozen untried growth ideas, try them (Airbnb tried cereal and conventions and didn't run out of zany ideas). If the best idea left is "maybe pay influencers," that is a better signal to pivot.
- A successful pivot gets warmer, closer to what you are an expert at, and builds on what you learned from the prior idea. "A good pivot is like going home."
- Examples he gives:
  - Brex began as a VR headset company run by Stanford dropouts who knew nothing about optics. They had earlier worked on a fintech company in Brazil, so he told them to work on what they know.
  - Retool came from cashew, a UK peer-to-peer payments app. The founders had built many internal dashboards to run it and in earlier internships.
  - PostHog knew analytics and had strong opinions on it.
  - Segment started as software for telling a professor you were confused in class, then became a Mixpanel competitor, then a JavaScript snippet that sends events to multiple endpoints. They could not have started with the final idea because they learned how analytics works by grinding on earlier ones.
- Sometimes founders resist the right idea because they are burnt out on it. They have to get over that barrier.
- In the winter 2017 batch, Brex and cashew looked like the two worst companies in his group of about 35-40. Both turned into Brex and Retool, the most successful in the group.

chunks.heading: Finding ideas: avoid the same information diet and tarpits
chunks.text:
- Founders share the same information diet (same podcasts, same Twitter accounts, same blog posts, same friends), so they land on the same ideas. His prompt: go off the beaten path, using your own experience or interests, so your exact person would come up with something others wouldn't.
- Trends become fashionable fast. Trucking startups were fresh because nobody did them and worked well, then became conventional wisdom.
- Zip's approach (his bespoke advice to Rul): find large public or private-equity-owned incumbents that are hated by their customers, where the software is horrible, and look for a knowable big market with a low-NPS incumbent. Rul had also run a marketplace, Flight Car, and was a strong executor. Zip went through about six pivots before landing there, and Dalton says his co-founder Lou deserves credit too.
- Tarpit ideas: ideas many people come up with, that seem like an unsolved problem, and that get lots of positive validation. That is different from a bad idea. Examples: an app to coordinate with friends where to go out at night; Foursquare clones (for years "Foursquare is going to own this," and now Foursquare is a B2B business); music discovery, which he worked on himself in his first startup.
- Founders get stuck because early validation is genuinely positive, and people have been starting these startups since the 90s.
- Market size: he says it matters more the later the stage. For pre-seed and YC applicants it matters little. Uber, Airbnb, and Razorpay (the largest payment processor in India, whose 2015 market was tiny because few used credit cards) all had tiny market sizes at the start. He cares more about "how do you get users, how do you grow, are you making something people want." He notes many investors still care about Tam, and says it is hard to win that debate.

chunks.heading: Talking to customers
chunks.text:
- Most founders know to talk to customers, but when he asks how many they talk to, "they get really quiet." The cause is mostly social anxiety and fear of looking stupid. Power through the awkwardness until it stops feeling bad.
- It has to be in person, not hiding behind a keyboard. Landing pages and Instagram ads to validate an idea are not talking to customers.
- Heuristic: look at your calendar. Roughly 20-30% of your time should say customer meeting or call (it varies by idea space), and the past month should show real physical meetings.
- Examples:
  - Brex and Retool sold inside the YC network.
  - Zip's founders cold-DMed people on LinkedIn asking how they felt about their procurement products, did hundreds of these, pre-sold before building, and the contacts became early beta testers.
  - PostHog launched open source, drew excitement on Hacker News, and had calendars full of people wanting to talk.
- The Collison install: when a customer says yes but goes quiet, don't let it churn. The Collisons would say "I'm in the neighborhood," show up, ask to drive the keyboard, and install Stripe into the customer's site, not leaving until it was implemented. His takeaway: even after a yes you are not done with sales; finish the last mile. Patrick also messaged him weekly on Google Talk when Dalton was an early Stripe customer.
- Getting started: do customer validation first, before a PowerPoint deck or fundraising. Pre-sell something before writing code. Build once you think at least one person would use it. Finding excited customers is "a great green light" to do the startup.

chunks.heading: Don't over-delegate, stay close to product
chunks.text:
- Common mistake: investors push founders to hire senior people with shiny big-tech resumes, or hire a PM or senior salesperson too early, or to "spend the money you raised." Two years later they realize they over-delegated and must clean it up. It is nobody's fault; the founder took their eye off the ball.
- His best product advice: founders who are great at product stay deep in the weeds, still care a lot, and still talk to customers at late stage. "You can't delegate caring about your users" or about the product being great.
- Time management: if you care about customers and product, your instincts on priorities are usually good. He would cut time spent hanging out with investors and networking first.
- Sales: founders afraid of sales think they need an expensive coach. His cheaper path is to read the most popular basic sales books on Amazon, such as Getting to Yes, plus Founding Sales (he recommends it for founders doing sales). He says that gets you about 80% of the way.

chunks.heading: Growth hacking is a waste of time very early
chunks.text:
- His contrarian view: growth hacking, analytics and A/B testing are a total waste of time for very early startups.
- Much online startup advice is aimed at Series A/B companies, and seed founders consume it and get confused. Split testing and feature flags make sense for a Facebook employee shipping small features on a product that already has scale, not for someone with no users.
- Imagine the original Airbnb founders, with four users whose names they knew, running complicated split-test growth theory.
- Instead, know your archetype, then look at what comparable companies did from zero to one and ignore what they do today. Examples:
  - Whatnot (a consumer marketplace) focused on the buy side and was intellectually honest about marketplace metrics rather than dumping money into Instagram ads.
  - Facebook got 100% penetration at Harvard first rather than launching broadly.

chunks.heading: What big founders have in common, and investor behavior
chunks.text:
- He doesn't think personality type matters. Very quiet and very extroverted founders, such as Tony from DoorDash, Grant from Whatnot, Patrick from Stripe and Ryan from Flexport, are all very different people.
- What they share: they really want it and believe in themselves, with something deep that says "I'm the one" and won't accept it not working despite employees and executives wanting to quit. It works like an internal gravitational force that bends the world to their will.
- Conviction is built, not innate at the start. Patrick wasn't sure Stripe would work until a year or two in. Conviction grows as customers and data reflect back that you're on track, creating a virtuous cycle.
- Why investors say no: put yourself in their shoes. They make few investments per year, so most "pretty good" deals get a no. There is usually no hidden truth, such as your Zoom setup or shirt color. They pick what they are personally most excited about or think can be phenomenally big.
- Careers are long and people reinvent themselves. He met Reid Hoffman when LinkedIn had about 12 employees, and knew Sam Altman as a young Stanford dropout working on Loopt. His own career went engineer, founder, product manager, then YC partner.
- YC's 2024 request for startups (a nudge to widen information diets, not a prescription) included ERPs (few applications, usually good ones), open source companies, space companies, ending cancer, spatial computing, defense technology, bringing manufacturing back to America, better enterprise glue (software connecting brittle business systems, which LLMs may improve), and small fine-tuned models as alternatives to giant generic ones.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton Caldwell draws on his imeem experience to explain why building a startup on licensed music content is structurally dangerous. He covers when lawsuits arrive, why acquisitions break down, why labels act rationally, and why depending on someone else's content means you don't control your company.

chunks.heading: Success is what triggers lawsuits in music and streaming content
chunks.text:
- Dalton says that if you work with music, "you're going to get sued. It's just a fact of life." Streaming content also draws patent trolls, as it does for everyone else.
- Founders often assume that no label email so far means the labels are fine with what they're doing, or that they like the "discovery platform." Dalton says the labels won't come talk to you until you have money and are successful.
- Labels keep a queue of startups they track, and they take screenshots. He says: "you just never want to get to the top of that queue," because once you do, they focus on you.
- Raising money and getting traffic are the moments the suit arrives.

chunks.heading: M&A is basically impossible for music startups
chunks.text:
- Without label deals, no acquirer will buy you. The huge legal liabilities would pass to the buyer, so the big company would be on the hook for a lot of money.
- With label deals, no one will buy you either, because the deals aren't transferable.
- Every label deal he has seen gives the labels a right of first refusal to pull the deal if they dislike the acquisition.
- He compares it to needing approval from all four major labels on top of your own board. The labels would look at the economics of the deal and decide whether they are fairly compensated.
- His conclusion: either way, an exit is tough.

chunks.heading: If you depend on someone else's content, you don't control the asset
chunks.text:
- This applies beyond music, to any large content company.
- If your survival depends on content someone else controls, "you effectively are not in control of the asset. It's not actually your company." You are a proxy through which they hold the asset.
- If the people who control the content don't like what you're doing, they can take you down or destroy you. He says he would not recommend that position to anyone.

chunks.heading: Why the labels' behavior is rational
chunks.text:
- Dalton says he didn't understand the labels until he spent a lot of time with them.
- Their industry went from about $15 billion in annual gross revenue and has been cut roughly in half. Executives (SVPs/EVPs) are paid to "fix" it while it shrinks every year.
- They are emotional about it: their friends keep getting laid off, and the labels have layoffs every few months. He describes real people with families whose entire industry is being burnt down.
- Their equation requires bringing in several billion dollars a year. A ramen-profitable startup that might make a few thousand dollars next year, pitching "get big first, focus on users, monetize later, Google AdWords in the meantime," isn't worth the salary cost of the conversation.
- So they hunt for the big win, "the touchdown pass, the buzzer beater," rather than licensing many small companies. He says he doesn't want their job and has sympathy for them.

chunks.heading: Structural incentives behind the "money transfer scheme"
chunks.text:
- For several years, music startups (and video content sites) have effectively been money transfer schemes. Money flows from VC funds (who take their fees) to startups to labels.
- It's good for the labels' bottom line. The margins on these cash deals are very good, and they don't have to pay the artists out of the advances.
- Label staff are paid for short-term cash, much like Wall Street. He compares it to the real estate bubble, where people optimized for their own short-term bonuses with no incentive to think long term.
- His view is that this is why labels now chase billion-dollar deals instead of licensing three-person startups, and he says he agrees with that choice at this point.

chunks.heading: His proposed fix: legal music APIs and statutory licensing
chunks.text:
- Developers need broadly available, legal music APIs to build on.
- He tried to provide one at imeem: he got a license and shipped a music/video API. It wasn't successful and is no longer on, and "people can't really build a company when something doesn't exist."
- He believes Congress has to get involved, as it did for Pandora and webcasters, with statutory licensing: a clear checklist, published rates, and a claim of the statutory license.
