- This would also stop long-tail rights holders (not owned by the labels, like the Beatles) from suing even after you've done label deals. They want their own publishing and masters, so they need to be in the statutory system too.
- It has to work internationally. Every European country has a different licensing body, each wanting its own advances and deal structures.
- His summary: the solution is similar to software, where the government has to get involved.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel clarify that a tarpit idea is not just a bad idea. It is one many founders keep independently having, that earns lots of praise, and that keeps failing. The list is not static: new technology like LLMs can reopen old ideas, so founders should explain what changed and talk to users.

chunks.heading: Dalton's definition of a tarpit idea
chunks.text:
- Dalton explains that YC kept seeing founders apply with the same idea over and over. YC often funded several of them, and the idea usually didn't work.
- The metaphor is the dinosaur tarpit: it looks like a pool of water from afar, the dinosaur goes to drink, and it gets stuck and dies. That is why tarpits are full of dead dinosaurs, and why these idea spaces are full of dead founders.
- He says the most common misreading is treating "tarpit" as a synonym for "an idea I don't like". Tarpit ideas are a small subset of ideas. Plenty of ideas are neither good nor bad, just normal.
- The tell is that other founders keep coming up with the same idea constantly. If they don't, it isn't a tarpit.
- It's not a static list. When technology changes, an old tarpit can become viable, and ideas he mocks now may stop being tarpits.

chunks.heading: Warning signs that an idea is a tarpit
chunks.text:
- Most startup ideas get honest skepticism from friends. Tarpit ideas get lots of praise, because nobody wants to discourage you.
- Example: a restaurant discovery app. The problem is "I can never decide where to eat", and friends all say "I have that problem all the time".
- It sounds too good to be true. If you're getting too much positive feedback, or it feels like "why does this not already exist, it seems so easy", that is not the shape of things that work. Dalton says to be a little skeptical.
- It has been done many times, many people have failed, and nothing has changed. Dalton says founders often avoid doing research so they don't learn things they don't want to learn.
- It is one of the first ideas to pop into people's heads, so there is an endless supply of people who haven't started a company yet and land on the same one.

chunks.heading: How LLMs change the analysis
chunks.text:
- Dalton says he is now open to classic tarpit ideas no longer being tarpits.
- What he wants to see: a founder who can explain why the new technology makes something possible that wasn't possible before.
- What he dislikes: a founder who doesn't acknowledge that many people have tried and failed. He jokes that for some founders history starts when they turn 18.
- Example: he funded a company doing fully AI-generated podcasts this batch. He says he would not have funded it before LLMs and voice generation, so he is in an "okay, let's see" phase.
- YC has funded generative video and audio companies since roughly 2016-2017, and he says quality keeps improving.
- His test: if you can't draw a connection between the technology and why your problem can be solved today, and the idea has been tried many times, that is tricky.

chunks.heading: "Co-pilot for X" is common, not a tarpit
chunks.text:
- Dalton separates common from tarpit. "Co-pilot for X" (real estate agents, lawyers, investment bankers, dentists, dog walkers) is a very common AI idea.
- It isn't a tarpit, because not enough people have tried it yet. It doesn't mean you shouldn't try it.
- It is the kind of idea people produce when they try to derive AI startup ideas from first principles.
- He says the point of the video isn't to crush anyone's dreams. Many people start companies to fix a problem they truly care about. The "depressing" lesson is that the current technology only addresses a certain set of problems, and each new chunk of technology means re-exploring which problems are addressable.

chunks.heading: Flavor 1: "The world should work differently"
chunks.text:
- The founder believes the way something works is bad, and everyone would have to adopt a new scheme at the same time.
- Example: coordinating with friends to see who is free to hang out, or event planning. It would be better if all your friends wanted to hang out all the time.
- It rests on everyone installing a new app to see what their friends are doing, and people don't seem to want that.
- Dalton says the idea comes from a good, utopian place. It runs into the fact that human behavior is very hard to change.
- He calls it a perfect tarpit because no one will tell you no.

chunks.heading: Flavor 2: Arbitrage and getting rich fast
chunks.text:
- The founder has secret knowledge or a limited window, and believes the right idea at exactly the right time lets them skip the usual 15 years it takes to build a startup.
- Dalton says this tends to lead to building whatever is currently raising money, or an arbitrage play. He cites a lot of adtech as an example.
- Example: during the pandemic, many startup ideas came straight out of r/WallStreetBets. One founder, doing well there, planned to quickly create an investment advisory business so friends could hand over their money.
- His reaction is that people forget markets don't only go up. He worries about the friends who put their life savings in.

chunks.heading: Takeaways and the question Dalton asks
chunks.text:
- Dalton's summary: the tarpit list isn't static, and ideas from the first video may no longer be tarpits. If an idea looks too good to be true, get skeptical.
- When founders ask him "is my idea a tarpit?", he asks whether they have talked to any users. They often haven't.
- His advice, as he describes it from YC's videos: talk to users and get a customer, rather than picking an idea based on a video.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton Caldwell, drawing on six years building imeem, walks through every music startup model (artist tools, download stores, ad-supported, subscription, unlicensed) and shows why the economics and deal structure usually fail. The durable lessons are opportunity cost, doing the unit-economics math early, and avoiding fixed contractual obligations.

chunks.heading: Why Dalton warns founders off music startups
chunks.text:
- Dalton built imeem, a music startup, and spent six years on it. He now calls the opportunity cost real: "if I would have spent that time building something else, probably better for me."
- Founders are drawn to music because everyone feels like an expert on taste. Many also think they will fix the labels single-handedly, or that "social music" is an aha idea.
- Traffic is easy to get. If you put up free unlicensed MP3s, users show up even if the product is bad. Dalton says this makes you feel smart, but it is a trap.
- His example is the original Napster: it "crashed a lot," but people kept using it because the music was free.

chunks.heading: Tools for artists: low margins, little money
chunks.text:
- Dalton says the "tools for artists" startup (Radiohead going direct to fans, "we don't need labels") is a very common and saturated category. Artists generally don't have money to pay.
- He points to Tunecore as a disruptive model: it charges a flat fee to put music in stores and takes no percentage of sales.
- He points to Topspin as strong, since its CEO manages the Beastie Boys and already has distribution for artist-to-consumer sales.
- The margin math on a store:
  - Best case is about 20% margins.
  - To make $50K a month to run a startup, you must sell about $250K of an unknown band's content every month.
  - Selling that much unknown-band MP3 content is, in his words, "the hardest thing I can possibly imagine."
- His advice: this is the one startup everyone does, so "don't do it."

chunks.heading: Download stores: advances and incumbents
chunks.text:
- Licensing deals with labels require advances, which Dalton puts at about $3-4 million up front. Elsewhere in the talk he says $5 million in with 20% margins means you'd need to sell about $25 million to pay back the capital.
- iTunes already holds 90%+ market share, and it is very hard to get people to switch where they buy music.
- Amazon is selling music for less, and Google was about to launch a music store.
- His verdict: "this is a really hard business."

chunks.heading: Ad-supported licensing: per-play and quarterly minimums
chunks.text:
- This is what Dalton did at imeem. His vision was to take the traffic that lived in peer-to-peer land and monetize it so everyone gets paid.
- Per-play minimums are widely criticized, and he agrees they are hard. You owe the labels on every play whether or not you showed an ad, so you can get upside down fast.
- The deadlier problem, which "no one writes about," is quarterly minimum advances:
  - You owe the labels millions every quarter no matter what, even if your site goes down.
  - You can't pivot out of deals like this. "You're boned."
- Labels may stop licensing ad-supported music at all. Free music on mobile devices removes the reason to own music, and cloud music further breaks their economics.

chunks.heading: Subscription startups: the unit economics
chunks.text:
Dalton's sarcastic recipe: spend two years in stealth doing deals, raise $5-6 million, and give labels 10-30% of the company. Then the business model:

- Charge $10 a month.
- Expect about 10% monthly churn, which he calls "the AOL effect."
- You keep roughly $3-5 of the $10, and he says he is being generous.
- That has to cover headcount, bandwidth, IT and customer acquisition, plus the quarterly minimums.
- International licensing is separate: each country has a different body to license with, so launching in more than one country is "insanely difficult." A social site limited to one country struggles to get network effects.
- Competition includes Rhapsody, Spotify, Audio, MOG, and the roughly $300 million of ads Rhapsody ran on MTV and VH1.

chunks.heading: Unlicensed or "DMCA-compliant" sites, and Pandora
chunks.text:
- Dalton does not recommend running an unlicensed site that takes down tracks on request. He has been sued himself.
- The human cost: when someone declares jihad on you in the press, you "don't want to come to the office." A process server knocking at 6 a.m. is "not badass, not cool."
- He says he has talked to founders who chose to shut down rather than face more litigation.
- DMCA radio, which is Pandora's route, looks decent:
  - They had to lobby Congress to keep it going and succeeded.
  - They make about $100 million in annual revenue and are close to profitable.
  - He still does not recommend it to very small startups.

chunks.heading: Why it is hard: structure, not people
chunks.text:
- Dalton says the problem is the legal structure, not the people. He compares it to software patent trolls.
- There are no clear rules for running a music startup, especially internationally. Lawyers tell you "you can do it or not, your call... do you feel lucky today?"
- This applies to mashups and to publishing: on top of paying the labels you also pay publishing, which he says he could talk about for three hours.
- "If you mess with music you're going to get sued. It's just a fact of life."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton explains why he launched Standard Capital with Paul Buchheit and Brian Berg: apply the YC seed model (short application, standard terms, founder-set price, fast answer) to the Series A. He argues fundraising is a time sink, valuation is made up, and founder peer groups beat board seats.

chunks.heading: Why Dalton started Standard Capital
chunks.text:
- He gives pivot advice by asking where a founder has the most unfair advantages and the best network. He believes "every person has a perfect idea for them" and that a partner's job is to pull it out of the founder.
- Standard Capital is his own version of that idea, designed for the founding team of Dalton, Paul Buchheit (PB) and Brian Berg.
- The thesis is to take what makes YC work at the seed stage and apply it to the Series A.
- His reasoning is that seed rounds changed completely over 20 years (the safe, a deep angel ecosystem, YC), while Series A has not changed since the 1980s.

chunks.heading: The Series A process he is trying to replace
chunks.text:
- When he raised a seed round 20 years ago, he needed a lead investor and a priced-round term sheet. He sold 25% of the company, gave up a board seat, and it took seven months. He calls getting it done "a miracle."
- His Series A was the same. He warmed up intros, kept investors in a CRM and went on coffee dates.
- Investors would spend weeks or months on him and say they were "definitely coming in," then pass at the very end, often silently.
- The fundraising meant he wasn't working on his startup. Paul Graham was the only one honest about it: do it in as little time as possible.
- Founders raising an A today describe the same experience.
- Decoding VC-speak is "so much of our job at YC":
  - Anything other than a clear yes is a no.
  - A long email full of words is a no.
  - He compares it to "a plate full of garnishes and just a no in the middle."
- He is sympathetic to VCs. They have to raise money from their own investors, so doing something different is the riskiest thing they can do.
- His diagnosis of the classic Series A investor: the business is relationship- and reputation-based. They invest where trusted people tell them to.

chunks.heading: Standard Capital's product: apply, standard terms, you set the price
chunks.text:
1. **A real application.** Anyone in the world can apply on a website, with no warm intro. It should take an hour or two, like a YC application. The point is to keep the founder's time cost and downside minimal. No one knows you applied, and the upside is getting money fast.
2. **A standard Series A term sheet, public on the website.**
   - That is where the name comes from.
   - Like the YC safe, anyone can read the terms before applying.
   - This replaces the usual pattern where the real terms show up at the end of the process, when the founder has no leverage.
3. **A fixed 10% for the lead check, with the founder naming the amount.** The application is a text box, for example "$6M for 10%." He says valuation has no equation: "Everyone just makes up numbers," and negotiation is like haggling at a flea market. This mirrors YC demo day, where founders set their cap and investors are in or out.
4. **A promised turnaround.**
   - The site will tell applicants how many days until a firm yes or no.
   - He admits this is hard to promise (vacations, hot deals to chase).
   - He argues a clear answer, even a no, beats being stretched out with "one more meeting" and "the partner meeting."
- He is explicit that he designed the process to be intuitive for YC founders.
- He also dislikes decks. Founders can spend a month on one and it is often still weak, and it is not the job. YC applications are all in one format, which makes them easy to read.

chunks.heading: Software at the center of the fund
chunks.text:
- His view is that YC was "a software company created by a person that loved software" and didn't love a lot of human process. Whenever there was a problem, PG built software for it, and much of YC's software traces back to that.
- Brian Berg ran a company with Dalton for over a decade, and Dalton introduced him to Patrick Collison when he started at YC. Brian became employee 70 at Stripe and has been an engineer there since. He is the software person on the Standard Capital team.
- Dalton says it was unusual to build software into an investing firm. A pitch deck in an inbox is not software-centric.
- Standard Capital is using AI in every decision it makes. He describes the firm as treating itself as "guinea pigs" to build an organization of the future and to be self-similar with its portfolio companies.
- He describes the launch as an MVP to improve over time, in the spirit of the YC goal of earning its 7% each year.

chunks.heading: No board seats, and a peer group instead
chunks.text:
- Standard Capital will not take board seats. His reasoning:
  - Founders don't want someone who might fire them.
  - It is awkward to ask for money from someone who might fire you.
  - There is no time to get to know them or pressure-test the relationship first.
- Instead, it will run quarterly subgroups, like YC group office hours.
  - Founders present their company metrics, board-update-style, and their biggest problems to each other.
  - He calls it a "group therapy thing."
- His argument: founders respect other operators in the trenches more than investors repeating stories they heard elsewhere. His example is Zuckerberg, who could call anyone. He has founders like Tony from DoorDash, Brian from Airbnb and Drew from Dropbox as directors. Dalton says that is who Zuck consults on running Facebook and on AI strategy, all YC people.
- The bar to join the peer group is product-market fit among AI builders. He says that is rare, since most batches mix companies at very different stages.
- He thinks investors overvalue both the money and their own advice. Standard Capital is built so value comes from the peer group instead. It will give advice, but "the value prop is not we're the best advice givers," and the biggest check does not always win.

chunks.heading: Non-zero-sum thinking about startups
chunks.text:
- He holds that PG's thinking is deeply anti-zero-sum. The zero-sum view is that only one good startup begins each year, and you are bad if you miss it.
- When YC started, many people predicted it would fund the worst startups, "a baseball team with all the worst baseball players."
- Dalton says PG was right that wealth and growth are not fixed and feed on each other. Many early YC companies, such as Twitch and Reddit, would not exist otherwise.
- His thesis is that there will be many more big companies, not one or two a year. Standard Capital funding more great founders creates more abundance and does not hurt other VC firms.
- He calls the zero-sum mindset common in the industry and "disappointing." Positive-sum thinking is "why tech exists."
- He notes that AI may lower how much capital companies need. His example is a profitable company at $8M in revenue wondering whether to raise at all.

chunks.heading: How to apply
chunks.text: - Apply at standardcap.com. The application and terms will be documented and transparent.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel unpack why Airbnb, Coinbase and Stripe worked. Each entered a market with bad incumbents, built something 10x better, was told by experts it was a dumb idea, and found the market bigger than they first thought. The lessons: ignore incumbents and non-user experts, build for users you know, and be careful with market-size math.

chunks.heading: Existing products existed, but were bad enough that a 10x version was possible
chunks.text:
- Dalton notes that people assume Airbnb, Coinbase and Stripe invented their categories. None did.
- Airbnb: he used VRBO before Airbnb existed. CouchSurfing was big and had mind share, so Airbnb felt like a "third-rate entrant to a crowded space".
- Coinbase: buying bitcoin around 2011 was miserable. One path meant sending money orders to a foreign country, which he skipped because it "seemed too much like a total scam".
- Stripe: accepting cards online was painful, and Stripe was a clear 10x improvement.
- His takeaway: in all three cases the founders had the problem themselves, had real experience with it, and saw an obvious opportunity for something 10x better.

chunks.heading: Airbnb: the contrarian takes that made it look like a bad investment
chunks.text:
- Dalton, speaking as an investor of that era, says there were two "bad idea" signals.
- Renting a room in a home where the host is present was seen as unappealing and scary. Older, wealthier people would not choose a stranger's Manhattan apartment over a nice hotel.
- Charging money was seen as uncool and impure. CouchSurfing's ethos was communal and pay-it-forward, and being commercial was "extremely in poor taste".
- The advice founders of that era were given: get huge first, with 100 million people, then monetize.
- His summary: "build something like couchsurfing but with no users... and you're going to charge money for it. Good luck." It sounded like a suicide mission.

chunks.heading: Coinbase: a simple fix for a terrible market, doubted even by its founder
chunks.text:
- Dalton lost some money (about one bitcoin) on Mt. Gox, which was the biggest exchange, kept going down, and got hacked. Money went in but didn't reliably come out.
- Buying bitcoin was something people wanted to do, but every option was bad. Coinbase wasn't the first mover, but the incumbent product was so poor that a 10x version was within reach.
- The objections at the time:
  - Bitcoin was seen as a tiny market, a bubble and a crash risk.
  - It was synonymous with fraud, and investors disliked it.
  - A US bank deal was seemingly impossible, which is why exchanges were offshore.
- Brian's own YC application leaned on a P2P-transfer idea, "something like PayPal". Dalton says even he under-weighted the core promise.
- That core promise was buying bitcoin in the US with a debit card, without being sketchy or getting hacked. In Dalton's words, "that was enough of an insight to be the basis for like a hundred billion dollar company".

chunks.heading: Stripe: a painful experience of his own, and a product built for developers
chunks.text:
- Dalton set up card acceptance twice before Stripe, in about 2002 and again in 2007.
- A merchant account was "like applying for a mortgage": lots of paperwork, faxing, personal guarantees, fraud checks, minimums, and expense. He calls it "gnarly and the opposite of easy in every way".
- He was among Stripe's first hundred beta customers, for his third company. When it appeared on Hacker News he wanted it before he had even seen it.
- Why Stripe won on go-to-market:
  - They built a beautiful website and beautiful documentation, and asked what a programmer would want.
  - Competitors targeted business buyers. Whoever implemented authorize.net was just someone paid to wire up code.
  - Developers freaked out about Stripe, and everyone copied its docs and site.
  - Dalton says "if Steve Jobs had to design a payments company it would be Stripe".
  - Stripe ran a beta invite program, which created buzz because access felt like a favor.
- The objections were that it was a crowded market with PayPal as an obvious threat, that regulation made it hard, and that it needed a bank deal.

chunks.heading: YC's early reputation and the lesson on being contrarian
chunks.text:
- Dalton recalls that the knock against YC at the time was that it "would just fund crappy versions of existing companies", meaning third-rate knock-offs of something good. He finds it hilarious in hindsight.
- His overarching theme is that all three founders had to be contrarian. Asking experts, investors or fellow founders would have mostly produced "that's stupid".
- The signals that mattered were:
  - the founders had the problem themselves
  - their smart friends complained about the same thing
  - the existing product was bad
  - the 10x improvement was within reach

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton and Michael Seibel explain the gap between investors dismissing YC publicly and funding YC companies constantly. The lesson for founders: understand each investor's incentives (first check, ownership, price) and weigh actions over talk.

chunks.heading: Why YC's investors quietly love it while publicly criticizing it
chunks.text:
- Dalton frames the video around the word "secretly". Investors often say on blogs and social media that YC "sucks" and that founders should go straight to their funds.
- Founders ask YC about this often: "an investor told me doing YC doesn't make sense for me."
- His point is the gap between what investors say to founders they are passing on and how they behave as investors.
- Investors who criticize YC publicly also invest in YC companies all the time.
- The stats he cites from the video, counting investments into YC companies:
  - a16z: 234
  - Sequoia: 139
  - Founders Fund: 104
- Anyone can check the YC top companies list and see who invested. Dalton says it is all the biggest firms, and they are voting with their pocketbooks.

chunks.heading: YC as a filter: the restaurant analogy
chunks.text:
- Dalton compares top VC firms to high-end restaurants. They like to give the impression that they go out to farms and hand-select the live chickens themselves.
- Most of what is on the menu comes from purveyors who find the best ingredients, prepare them and deliver them "in a nice box in a nice package".
- Dalton says that with so much demand, it makes sense for these firms to prefer things pre-selected and packaged. That is the service YC provides to VCs.
- The packaging is better for two reasons. YC companies tend to be further along than the average company walking in, and more technical.

chunks.heading: Why the love stays secret: the "first check" conflict
chunks.text:
- Dalton points out that VCs also say "we want to be your first check". That clashes with their love of YC companies.
- Why it stays secret, as he frames it:
  - VCs would rather be the first check.
  - They know that if a company does YC, they won't be.
- Dalton calls it "a really tricky game".
- His position is that, whatever they say, the top investors cannot pass on a really great company. "If they need YC because they're smart", they invest.

chunks.heading: Seed funds have a different squeeze
chunks.text:
- Dalton asked how seed funds fit into this dynamic.
- He says seed funds are more limited than traditional VC funds. A VC that misses your A can still do your B or C.
- A seed fund knows its main chance to invest in you is the first round, and that it will be diluted after that. That is why it tries to get as big a chunk as possible at as low a price as possible.
- Seed funds have still written thousands of checks into YC companies, but at higher prices.
- You can't really blame seed funds for discouraging YC, given those dynamics.

chunks.heading: How founders should weigh investor advice
chunks.text:
- Dalton's framing is that the people marketing to you are running businesses with their own incentives, and so is YC.
- Founders should understand those dynamics and make the best decision for their own company.
- The key question when someone gives you advice about YC is whether they are offering to invest.
- Dalton's closing line is: "spend a little bit more time looking at what people do rather than what they say or they meme or they tweet." The best YC companies were funded by the best VC firms and seed funds.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel describe the two failure modes of founder mindset: too pessimistic (quitting after one bad signal) and too optimistic (magical thinking detached from how the world works). Dalton argues founders must hold both views at once, stay rooted in reality, and not expect funding, hires or trends to rescue an unproven startup.

chunks.heading: Magical thinking: the founder failure mode Dalton warns about
chunks.text:
Dalton defines "magical thinking" as his own founder version of the psychology term. It is believing you live in a world with magical causes and effects, where things not rooted in reality are true for you. He calls it a poor grasp of how the world actually works.

- Example: believing that if you pitch a famous investor in an airport, he will instantly see your brilliance, "get out of his checkbook" and fly you away to become the next Google.
- Another version: treating life like a romantic comedy where you are the main character and a dramatic, showy act will make things work out.
- Dalton's contrast: the real way to meet an investor is to apply to YC on the website. "We're just normal people," and the path is "actually pretty straightforward."
- Founders who think this way often assume funded companies "got lucky like that," so they copy the luck instead of studying how the world really works.

chunks.heading: How magical thinking shows up in founders' behavior
chunks.text:
- **Excuses:** Direct questions get long, complicated answers about why they can't grow or get customers. The story always casts the founder as the hero and external parties as the villains.
- **"If only I had money":** They tell stories about other companies getting breaks, or believe the next break will take them from zero to 100 in one step. Dalton finds this "extremely frustrating" because it misunderstands how the game works.
- **Product:** A founder with no tech co-founder who has never built a product and given it to anyone, yet thinks things are going well, is too optimistic. Dalton's blunt line: "it's not going well."
- **Idea worship:** Many founders pitch a social network that "is like Facebook and TikTok" with no code and no product. They are frustrated when YC isn't excited, because they assume the idea itself has inherent value.

chunks.heading: Over-optimism after raising money or hiring
chunks.text:
- **Money as a savior:** Raising from famous investors does not mean problems stop existing. Dalton sees founders turn off their brains after a raise: "we're on easy street, we nailed it."
- **Investors aren't magical:** Founders assume their investors have powers that will save the company. They don't.
- **The magic-hire fantasy:** Founders with a big, hairy problem they don't understand (usually pre-product-market-fit) assume a marketing or sales hire will come in and solve it. The belief is that they will "do it," not that you'll figure it out together.
- This is over-optimistic on two fronts: employees won't hand you the answer, and the best marketer in the world wouldn't join a pre-MVP startup anyway.

chunks.heading: Chasing hot categories
chunks.text:
- Dalton's pattern: founders assume an idea will work because it is trending or investors are talking about it on Twitter.
- Example: the flood of remote-work and video-conferencing startups when COVID hit. Zoom had been working for years and had a head start in technology and position. Starting from scratch after the moment arrives means optimizing for something that happens later.
- Rule: get in before everyone thinks it's cool, not at the peak.
- Signal an idea has "jumped the shark": it becomes one of the most common ideas people apply to YC with. His example is chatbots, which everyone built for a couple of years.

chunks.heading: Too pessimistic: what it looks like and how to diagnose it
chunks.text:
Dalton's rule: you need to be both optimistic and pessimistic, and if you are too far toward either extreme you will fail.

- **Core cause:** poor expectation setting. Founders don't realize the work is hard, and that even when it works you mostly get "no's."
- **Typical trigger:** a founder sends an unpersonalized cold email to 100 prospects, gets five replies and decides the startup doesn't work. Dalton notes YC hears this "every batch" and has to say "it's going to be fine."
- **Anything short of unmitigated success** right out of the gate makes them want to quit.
- **Giving god-like predictive power to one opinion:** a single investor, friend or customer saying it won't work.
- **Missing the point of aggressive goals:** founders treat missing a Demo Day goal as proof the company is dead. The goal exists to make you move fast. If you learned a lot pursuing it, you got the value even if you missed it.
- **Other signals:** giving up too early, expecting it to be easy, believing everyone else has it easier, and leaving people deflated after talking to you.
- Dalton says pessimism is curable, because the fix is usually to set realistic expectations.

chunks.heading: Holding both at once: the balance
chunks.text:
- Dalton invokes cognitive dissonance: holding two conflicting ideas at the same time, which most people find uncomfortable.
- The best founders can do it. Example: "My star employee just quit and says my startup is horrible and I don't know what I'm going to do, but I'm going to get on the sales call and sell my heart out and close this customer."
- Every day brings crises and victories. Founders who fail resolve the dissonance by going too far in one direction: freaking out over bad things or losing contact with reality.
- Many strong founders don't enjoy this but learn to thrive and execute in it, and the risk sharpens them. Many don't bring their true A-game until things are pretty bad.
- Blueprint in Dalton's words: be optimistic, just don't be magically optimistic, and stay "squarely rooted in real reality."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel walk through types of investors (finance, big-company exec, non-tech entrepreneur, junior, influencer, founder, young scout) and how each one's background skews their advice. The takeaway is that nobody, YC included, can tell a founder how to win, so founders must own the outcome and use advisors selectively.

chunks.heading: Investors can't fix your company, and some founders don't want to hear it
chunks.text:
- Dalton says telling founders this is "like telling them Santa Claus isn't real."
- Founders get time with him and ask what to do because no one wants their product. His honest answer is often "I have no idea."
- As a founder he believed that once he raised from top investors, they would hand over the secrets the world was hiding. He says that belief was wrong.
- Many investors have never been founders, so they haven't "been humbled by having a crappy startup" the way he and Michael were. It is easy for them to think their advice can make companies work, as if they were the magician.
- Over the years he has seen YC founders follow such advice and make very common errors. He can trace the mistake back to the type of person who gave the advice.

chunks.heading: The finance-background investor: "when all you have is a hammer"
chunks.text:
- Dalton describes this investor as someone who has never run or operated inside a company.
- If what you know is money, the solution usually involves money: raise more, spend more, "throw money at the problem."
- Example: being asked pre-product-market-fit for five-year financial projections. He says his reaction was "what's a financial projection?"
- Financial projections can make sense at a later stage. Pre-PMF, the real problem is that the company makes no money and spends money every month.
- He says the pattern shows up as founders who treat product as an afterthought and do financial engineering instead.

chunks.heading: The big-company exec investor
chunks.text:
- People with big-tech experience are great at taking a successful product and scaling or refining it.
- Being employee 100 or 200 at a big company is a very different job from being employee 5. Scaling a product looks like scaling a process, such as hiring.
- That mindset can take for granted that getting any users at all is hard. Failure for many YC companies means getting zero real customers, and a big-company PM mindset doesn't consider that you can fail that badly.
- Their typical advice is to hire executives before product-market fit, such as a marketing exec because "marketing doesn't work" or a VP of engineering because the team isn't productive.
- Pre-PMF the mistake is more often the wrong person in the company, not a missing department. Examples are an engineer no one wants to work with, or no one measuring marketing results.
- After product-market fit, hiring more people becomes essential.

chunks.heading: The non-tech entrepreneur, the junior investor and the influencer
chunks.text:
**Non-tech entrepreneur**
- Someone who made money in real estate, strip malls or franchises may treat a startup like a franchise store. They ask for crazy terms and more control, and stress that you'll lose their money.
- Dalton says you can't be mad at them. They are applying principles that worked for them in a different industry, and software companies look different from most other companies.

**Junior investor**
- His mental model is to put yourself in their shoes. New investors aren't in a position of power, and a few bad early investments can end a career.
- Their KPI is that you raise a follow-on round at a higher valuation so they can mark up the investment.
- So they push you to fundraise constantly and tell you everything is working, that you have product-market fit and should scale faster. They aren't trying to hurt you.

**Influencer or famous person**
- Influencers understand distribution because building it is their business. They treat startups like ad deals: advisor shares in exchange for promotion.
- It is tempting to think a celebrity tweet will fix distribution. In his experience, both personally and across YC, founders mostly feel they got a raw deal. The clicks were less helpful than hoped.

chunks.heading: The extremely young investor
chunks.text:
- These people are sweet and exciting to talk to.
- Dalton compares them to founders who learn how to "play the part" of a founder from movies and books. These investors read what other investors say and do, then repeat the hot trend or the latest essay.

chunks.heading: YC partners give bad advice too
chunks.text:
- Dalton names the common YC-partner advice: the lean-startup path of not hiring, not spending much, talking to users and shipping a rough MVP.
- Sometimes a team builds in a cave for two years without talking to a single user, and it works. The data on YC companies makes it hard to recommend that strategy.
- The best partners are careful how forcefully they give advice. Over time you build a record of times you told someone to do X and the opposite worked.
- His takeaway to Michael is that the founders who made it work believed in themselves. They took bits of outside information but took personal accountability for making it work, and didn't blindly follow anyone, YC included.

chunks.heading: The best investor advice Dalton ever got
chunks.text:
- As a founder he was "swimming in his head" with too many ideas and too much data.
- Someone from the outside looked at everything and synthesized it into something simple: "this is working, you should do more of this," or the opposite, "this is bad, you're failing."
- His brain was full of excuses and a thousand threads going in different directions. Having someone boil it down was hugely valuable.
- Looking back, the founder advice that helped most, for both him and Michael, came when people were hard on them. That was more hopeful than being told everything was great.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton and Michael argue pre-PMF startups should ignore growth graphs and weekly growth targets, and focus on a ladder of real users who love the product (1, 10, 50, 100). Gmail and Stripe show great products start slow and obsessively served. Building for investors instead of users is a trap.

chunks.heading: Goals before product-market fit: measure love, not growth graphs
chunks.text:
Dalton argues that the tools and habits from post-PMF companies (Meta-style analytics, AB tests, weekly growth targets) have no relation to tracking progress in an early-stage company. His point is that graphs are a waste of time when you have zero users.

- With three users who all churned, he says you effectively have zero users, so weekly growth is the wrong thing to talk about.
- Founders who learned analytics at big companies sometimes have to unlearn "all this crap" first.
- He notes that growing 7% week over week is the result of doing many things right, but founders treat it as the cause of the company working. Mixing those up "really screw[s] you up".
- His advice: "Don't even worry about graphs and charts and weekly growth. Just get something that someone loves."

chunks.heading: Founders cheat metrics, and it only hurts them
chunks.text:
Dalton describes a pattern where founders pick metrics that let them hit a target without reflecting reality.

- Example: using cumulative users who ever signed up instead of daily active users, ignoring whether anyone actually uses the product.
- He calls this Goodhart's law in practice (founders "doctor the metric so that they hit it"), and says "all you're doing is screwing yourself."
- He asks founders a gotcha question: to get value out of the product in a week, how much time should a user spend in it? Then: how much time are they actually spending?
- The answers he expects are "we're not measuring" or "an hour a week" when they claimed an hour a day. He then asks whether the product is helping users in their business or goals at all.
- Following that line of questioning usually ends at "we actually have zero users", and he says that is fine: "I'm glad we had that little chat."

chunks.heading: Build something a few people love (the Gmail example)
chunks.text:
Dalton says "it's almost impossible" for something a hundred people love to not be growing. Either the love is exaggerated or nobody is looking at the growth.

- He cites Paul Buchheit's Gmail as the model. Paul built it for himself and was the first user.
- He then gave it to people inside Google, adding only one or two a week and asking what to add.
- It stayed under 100 users for months, because he wanted people to love it. By the time it was in beta, hundreds of people "ran their life off it."
- Dalton's takeaway: "This is how you build great products." The most popular consumer product in the world did not start by chasing a hockey-stick graph.
- He admits it sometimes takes time to get someone to love a product, and time to work out what to build.

chunks.heading: Don't build your startup for investors
chunks.text:
Dalton pushes back on the "I have to fundraise in n months and investors love graphs" mentality.

- His view: building to impress investors means your actual customer is an investor, and "nothing good will come of that."
- You can win a seed round that way if you are smart and capable, but he notes only about a 2% chance of ultimately winning even after raising a seed round, so you have just taken your odds to roughly 98% failure.
- The alternative is to spend that same time with customers, testing hypotheses and learning how to improve their businesses and lives.
- He says he has seen many founders who fundraised poorly at demo day, had about half a million dollars from YC, powered through, and a year later were doing far better than batchmates who had built for investors.
- It is also habit-forming in a bad way. A "we'll worry about investors now and talk to users after we raise" culture sticks.

chunks.heading: Real company stories: Stripe and early customer obsession
chunks.text:
Dalton uses Stripe as the counterexample to the fast-growth narrative.

- Stripe is a company that YC talks about a lot. It is a hundred-billion-dollar company that didn't launch publicly for over two years.
- It was invite-only and beta-only, built first for the founders' own side product, with customers added very slowly.
- The Collison installation: they would sit down at your computer and help you implement Stripe into your payments flow.
- Dalton was an early Stripe customer at his own startup (among the first couple hundred customers). Patrick Collison messaged him on Google Talk nearly daily asking how it was going, which made him feel like an important customer who could reach the CEO directly.
- He calls that closeness a superpower founders don't talk about.
- His challenge: use AI to research how your top 10 favorite companies actually started. How long until launch, until 100 users, until $1M in revenue? "You're going to be shocked" that the real stories differ from the pop version.
- He says the fastest-to-$100M graphs are not the real race. The goal is enduring value and enduring businesses, not flash-in-the-pan growth.

chunks.heading: Dalton's goal ladder for pre-PMF companies
chunks.text:
Dalton's answer to "how do I set goals before PMF" is the progression used at YC, based on counts of users who love the product.

1. Do you have more than zero users?
2. Do you have one real user, with no asterisks?
3. Do you have 10?
4. Do you have 50?
5. Do you have 100?

- If you can get 100 users or customers who love you, "that is an awesome goal," and that is the point where he'd start graduating to graphs.
- He tells founders to be honest with themselves and use the word "love": how many users love my product? If none, what would cause them to?
- Staring at graphs all day is dehumanizing to your users. If you aren't thinking about the people you serve and whether they love you, "you're hurting yourself."
- On Whatnot, he says value was easy to see: sellers were making so much money that it was life-changing, an obvious sign the product provided value.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton and Michael Seibel argue that aiming small is the hidden killer of venture-backed startups, because big missions attract customers, hires and investors who care. They stress that ambition must come with a simple, credible pitch rooted in real knowledge, and warn against funding-cycle noise and scenesters.

chunks.heading: Low ambition is the secret killer of startups
chunks.text:
- Dalton frames the topic as "the thing that I believe is the secret killer of startups. And it's not what you expect. It is low ambition."
- His basis is that he and his co-host work with a lot of startups, and he says he has seen what happens when a company has low ambition.
- He calls the failure mode counterintuitive. Founders hear how hard startups are and how few succeed, so they try to raise their odds by aiming lower. A small startup seems easier than "the next Google, which sounds very hard."
- He says the evidence suggests that is not the case.

chunks.heading: Ambitious ideas often come from curiosity, not insider access
chunks.text:
- Dalton argues that most people watching can be curious about an area that "seems perhaps far-fetched, but if it went the right way could change the world."
- He says this is less hard than it sounds:
  - Ten years ago AI was not a buzzword, but working out who the leading AI researchers and the leading papers were was only a question of curiosity.
  - Understanding how broken NASA was is described the same way.
- He says the right area might not be in the zeitgeist, and that this "might actually be a good thing" because it could be the opportunity.
- His contrast: "building the 17th AI SDR might raise you your $2 million seed round", but that is not the same as picking something that could matter.

chunks.heading: Ambition is for venture-backed companies
chunks.text:
- Dalton's framing is for companies raising venture capital. A low-ambition idea can still be funded in a hot market, so funding is a poor way to judge whether an idea is ambitious.
- Ambition here means a mission that could change the world, not a small optimization.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton Caldwell and Michael Seibel argue that with AI tools making building cheap, the scarce thing is a genuinely unique idea. Copying funded companies or VC consensus gives derivative ideas; look at ideas others discarded, work from your own weirdness, and expect people to call it bad.

chunks.heading: Unique startup ideas come from the discard bin, not from what's currently cool
chunks.text:
Dalton's core claim: the bottleneck has moved from building to having an idea, and most ideas are not unique.

- Tools are now so good that "you can crank out anything." The scarce thing is a real idea.
- Many founders are pushed toward ideas that "sound good to investors" or toward the current Twitter trend. His example: cloning whatever is hot at the moment of recording (he names OpenClaw). He calls this "pretty low effort."
- Everyone has a similar filter for startup ideas. If your process is to find something that is both good and that no one has thought of, "you're going to have a bad time."
- His alternative: find an idea that has already been discarded by others for some reason. Instead of looking for what no one has thought of, "find something that everyone's thought of and thinks is bad."
- Instacart is the classic example of an idea that sat in the discard bin.

chunks.heading: Why copying funded companies is not validation
chunks.text:
Dalton speaks from 12 years of funding companies at YC.

- Founders interviewing at YC would say a company from two batches earlier doing the same thing "validates the market."
- His reaction: he funded that company, and he did not fund it for that idea. It pivoted during the batch. "There's no signal here."
- Reading the tea leaves of what launches in YC batches is "not a marketplace of picking ideas that have been de-risked."
- Seeing that something raised money at a billion-dollar valuation does not de-risk your idea either.
- Deciding what to spend the next 10 to 20 years on by looking at a list of what others are working on is a weak basis for a decision.

chunks.heading: Move away from consensus, including the VC content you consume
chunks.text:
- Non-consensus is the point. Move away from the consensus of startup founders, investors, and friends and family.
- Many successful YC companies had every friend and family member think the idea was bad (the Airbnb parents story came up in the conversation).
- Dalton's examples of deeply weird starts: OpenAI began as a non-profit research lab during the rise of SaaS and had no real product for a long time. Anthropic was "super weird," and a lot of its early money came from FTX. Both are now consensus winners, but they began as "the definition of non-consensus things."
- His caution: these are not recipes. Copying what worked for others will not give you a truly unique idea.
- VC content (including his own podcasts) is part of the problem. He says they have tried not to tell founders what to think, only to tell stories and give advice, like office hours for a wider group. But "if you're making all of your life decisions based on podcasts, that is a definition of coming up with ideas that are not unique."
- Before TechCrunch, startups had almost no coverage. Early-2000s founders had no VC content to anchor on.

chunks.heading: Big-TAM thinking filters out the best ideas
chunks.text:
- A common talking point is that only $100 billion or trillion-dollar outcomes matter. Dalton says this kills truly unique ideas, since they would never fit that framework.
- Whatnot, one of his better YC investments, is "a marketplace for authenticated Funko Pops." He asks "What's the TAM on that?" and says you would discard it.
- Applying late-stage investor advice to idea selection means only a small set of ideas pass, and those end up "extremely derivative repetitive ideas."

chunks.heading: Weird people have an easier time generating unique ideas
chunks.text:
- Non-conformist or quirky people constantly generate strange ideas and do not need to ask permission. Society tells them to stop, but they tend to do well in startups because they have no trouble with unique ideas. Their bigger problem is deciding which idea is worth their time.
- Systems are "consensus machines." People good at calibrating and triangulating consensus often find it hardest to come up with unique ideas, because it has been trained out of them.
- Y Combinator itself is his example. Most fund founders have investment careers and MBAs. Paul Graham built a Lisp website, got rich, and made up a summer program for young founders from first principles. He had no investor training, and the normal VCs now look up to him.

chunks.heading: If you can't come up with unique ideas
chunks.text:
- Dalton says it is "totally okay to go work somewhere." Not everyone has to be "a weird shaman that comes up with strange ideas," and society would not work if everyone were.
- You can also join a founder who is weird and let them come up with the idea.
- If you do start something, brace for it: working on something many people think is a bad idea is "100% the experience of everyone that's succeeded."

chunks.heading: What he looks for as an investor, and his stance on judging ideas
chunks.text:
- He is excited when a founder seems willing to stay for a couple of years. When he gets the vibe that a founder will move on if it doesn't work in a couple of months, that is a turn-off. His phrase: "you're 10% in, but you want me to be 100% in?"
- Don't seek approval from authority figures, including the hosts: if your filter is whether the people in these videos would approve of your idea, "we're saying no."
- He says they regularly funded ideas and worked with founders whose ideas they thought were bad. He compares his job to a doctor treating whoever walks in: "who am I to know whether this is going to work?"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Growth fixes many startup problems like fundraising and burnout, but fast growth can hide serious ones. Dalton and Michael list what founders should probe when growing fast: unit economics at each scale, defensibility, vision, real customer usage and hiring quality.

chunks.heading: Dalton's framing: what growth doesn't solve
chunks.text:
Dalton opens by saying the advice to "grow, grow, grow" stays, but with nuance. Growth fixes a lot: burnout, not being able to raise money, motivation.

- He is not knocking growth. His point is that fast growth does not automatically fix everything.
- The trigger for the topic is AI-related companies seeing "shocking growth" whose other problems may remain.
- At YC, the standard advice is a graph that goes up and to the right. To convince an investor, you convince them the existing trend will continue. He still thinks that is good advice.
- He wants founders who are experiencing growth to ask themselves some harder questions.

chunks.heading: Unit economics don't fix themselves with scale
chunks.text:
Dalton's first question for a growing company is about unit economics.

- His thought experiment is a "free money website" that pays you a dollar for every 75 cents of revenue. It would grow reliably while losing money.
- Losing money to get something off the ground can be a sophisticated, valid strategy.
- But "just growing faster doesn't mean you're going to solve uneconomic issues."
- He says more companies die by assuming economies of scale exist, without probing whether they ever arise in their own business.
- Classic example: growth bought with heavy ad spend, with a hoped-for payback period and no retention data yet. Ad-supported growth does not mean the problems are solved.
- On CAC: he has "never seen" a company whose cost to acquire a customer stays the same if it 100x's its marketing budget.
- Unit economics assumptions made at small scale need to be reassessed at every order of magnitude of scale, because they often change.
- Internet businesses often get worse economics as they scale because of hidden costs. Customer service and fraud are the ones that bite and that you never see early.
- Once fraud rings spend time attacking you, it is a "high class problem", but it is still hard.

chunks.heading: Moats: fast growth is not a moat
chunks.text:
Dalton's second question is about defensibility.

- He has seen people grow very fast with no idea how to make it defensible.
- His thought experiment: why won't a YC company in the next batch see that your thing is working and do exactly the same thing? What stops them taking your customers?
- Historical example: ad-tech style businesses that are a thin layer between many customers and a very large social media site. The large site may decide it wants a direct relationship with the customer.
- He does not demand an A+ answer all the time. His point is only that "it is not self-evident that because you are growing fast, you have a moat."
- The advice is to probe yourself and ask the hard question before a future competitor does.

chunks.heading: Be your own critic when things go well
chunks.text:
Dalton argues the meta-reason to ask these questions is that no one else will.

- Investors seeing revenue go up and to the right, employees, and the press will all say "great."
- At an inflection point, "you have to be your biggest critic," because no one else will do that work.
- He contrasts the two states of mind: when things aren't going well you have to be your own biggest fan, and when things are going well you have to be your own biggest critic. They are very different.
- It is hard to play that role without becoming "deputy downer" in your own company, especially while everyone is celebrating mega valuations.

chunks.heading: Vision: a hockey stick doesn't give you a picture of the company
chunks.text:
Dalton says growth does not force you to have a clear picture of what the company should become.

- He sees positive correlations between founders who have a very clear picture in their head of what the company is supposed to be and success. Others, when asked about far-future expectations, draw a blank.
- On his own work at Standard Capital: "I have a very clear picture about what I want it to be. I don't know if it'll work or not, but I can promise you, I can see it." His job is to manifest what he sees in his head.
- Example: Tony Xu of DoorDash. In office hours, when DoorDash was two months old, he could explain what it was supposed to be, and that is what it became. He kept referring to Amazon, and over the years he did it. At one point he said DoorDash was a given percentage of Amazon's daily deliveries, which was large.
- Founders with a vision have almost a philosophy: a somewhat odd explanation of what customers want and how to serve them over a long time, and they can "nerd out" about the company in depth.
- He says he truly had that experience at YC. He saw YC as a "100-year institution", a combination of a university, a VC fund and a software company. Paul Graham had a clear picture; many investors just see a well-paid job.
- Advice to a fast-growing startup: assume you have a competitor who thinks like that. The folks with the clearest picture are probably going to win.
- As you hockey-stick, you stop competing with little startups and start competing with the companies that make up the economy, and those have in-depth visions. If you have no vision, your work may just further their business model, for example when they bundle the best startup ideas in a space into their product.

chunks.heading: Hiring and customer value under fast growth
chunks.text:
Dalton flags two traps that come with growth.

**Hiring**
- Companies growing fast make bad hiring decisions, which he says comes from unclear thinking.
- Advising a company in a crisis, people want to hear that hiring one specific person or doing steps one, two and three will put out the fire. His reply is that "there are no firemen": the goal was to live in the fire, and that is what winning looks like.
- His examples: Tony (DoorDash) and Brian (Airbnb) are "in the fire."
- Growth makes hiring harder, not easier. When you aren't growing you mostly can't hire, and when you are, impressive-looking people suddenly want to join.
- Story: at a friend's high-flying company, an employee who didn't know who he was said they had picked five winning companies and planned to spend 18 months at each to pass the vesting threshold. His reaction: a taker, not a contributor, and easy to miss when growing fast.

**Not actually solving the customer's problem**
- Growing fast does not mean you are solving the customer's problem. The longer you grow, the more evidence accumulates that you are, but it is not proof.
- B2B SaaS example: a company sold a number of seats, but how many of the people with seats actually use the product? The innocent answer is "how would we know?" The darker answer is "we're working on retention."
- Software is often purchased in a company that no one wants or uses, and later un-purchased. He says this is common and rarely talked about, especially when a company is riding the zeitgeist.

chunks.heading: The founder's personal life isn't fixed by growth
chunks.text:
Dalton's last item: growth does not fix, and can worsen, a founder's day-to-day life.

- Health or personal problems are not solved by growth. A big stressor in your life stays.
- Growth demands more of your day-to-day resources for the company, so if you were just holding on, things get harder.
- He recalls a conversation with the former YC batch director, who said growth is an emotional struggle. Looking back, he realized that his now-wife had been with him through almost his whole startup journey, and he took that support for granted.
- "Your life gets exposed a little bit when you're growing and when your company's demanding more."
- His closing note: growth is still good and still the main thing. These are issues to flag if you are growing well. They are all fixable if you look at them, but "one of them is going to get you" if you put blinders on, because there are "too many stray bullets around."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton and Michael frame every startup negotiation around leverage: do you bring more value than you ask for, and could you walk away? Growth and a deep pipeline beat pitch decks, negotiation tricks and press. The pre-work is where the win happens.

chunks.heading: Leverage is the frame behind fundraising, sales, hiring and marketing
chunks.text:
Dalton's core idea from his YC years is that most founder questions ("how do I raise a good round", "how do I hire good people", "what should be in my pitch deck") are really questions about leverage. When a founder asked, he would stop them and ask "how much leverage do you have?", because the answer carried far more weight than a better deck or a better process.

- Leverage means: take whatever audience you are dealing with and ask whether you deliver more value than you ask for.
- A related definition is your ability to walk away. The more badly you need a thing to happen, the less leverage you have.
- He says negotiating is "10 times easier" when you have leverage. The advice is to ask in every negotiation how much leverage you have and what you can do to bring more to the table.
- Many young founders carry over their school experience, where teachers and institutions invest time and attention in you with little expectation of return. They expect investors and customers to behave the same way. Dalton says the startup world is a different one, where you must bring something of value.

chunks.heading: Fundraising: grow first, and a bad fundraiser with traction beats a great one without
chunks.text:
Dalton says one of the most misunderstood aspects of Y Combinator is that people think it is fundraising school, where partners teach you to pitch for three months and build hype. He says he would never have worked a decade at a place that was that.

- The real model, which he credits to Paul Graham: the way to be effective at fundraising is to grow so quickly and have so many proof points that you could be bad at fundraising, put very little effort in, and do it in a short time frame.
- Counterintuitively, doing it "seat of your pants" at the very end beats doing a lot of prep.
- His line: it is "way better to be like a very bad fundraiser with something that's working than someone that's a very good fundraiser with something that's not working at all."
- Investors see so many pitches that they are expert at spotting polished language. A founder's time is better spent making a good product, launching and talking to users.
- If you are not growing and not launched, working on the deck can be the biggest waste of your time. He says the deck isn't doing the work.
- Titles of slides are the wrong frame. The real question is whether you are growing, and how fast.
- He asks founders to estimate how many hours they spent raising a seed round, and how much more value they would have created spending those hours on the startup.

chunks.heading: Wasted time in fundraising, and why Standard Capital caps founder effort
chunks.text:
Dalton describes long fundraising processes as a drag on the industry. Low-leverage founders pitch for months with almost no chance of it working, and would have been better off not fundraising at all.

- He gives a "dark game theory" explanation for investors stringing founders along: an investor keeps meeting a founder to hold an option, so that if the company takes off they are well positioned. That process harms the founder's ability to reach the growth inflection point. He says he is "so not aligned with that."
- At Standard Capital he cannot fund everyone, and most applicants will not be funded. But he can calculate how much time they spent on the application and the interview, and he is comfortable that it is capped. He wishes more investors were judicious with founders' time.
- He sees this as an advantage YC has demonstrated in public for 20-plus years that has not been copied. He suggests both sides want to believe that spending lots of time with a non-growing company reveals subtlety a short set of meetings cannot, and says "that's certainly not the bet I would take."
- He describes long diligence on non-growing companies as "torturing everyone to find the diamond in the rough", a dead-weight loss on the industry. Most of the time, he says, a VC is investing on traction and chasing.

chunks.heading: Sales: you can't need any one deal
chunks.text:
Dalton says first-time founders treat an impressive inbound email (his example is someone from Google) as "we made it" and think they only need to close one deal. His position is that you can't need any single deal.

- High leverage is having so much inbound that you can be picky and choosy. Example: launch a product, get 1,000 signups, segment them by customer type, and decide whom you will serve (for example, skip enterprise).
- With no signups and one possible customer, you put all your eggs in that basket. Bad second-order effects follow: you can't tell whether you are near product-market fit or whether this one customer is weird, you get pushed into custom work, and the customer knows they have you. You may move further from PMF without realizing it.
- He notices that founders with a hot deal often stop doing outreach, telling themselves that landing it makes everything easy, or that they are too busy. In reality they are taking about one meeting a week.
- A test for leverage: if any deal dies, how much do you care? With leverage the reaction is "oh well, we've got eight others in the pipeline."
- Customers dislike feeling the company needs them more than they need the company.
- With leverage you can be aggressive on pricing, avoid discounts, and get a signed contract rather than an LOI. Strong companies even fire customers outside their ICP, saying in effect "you're paying us a lot, but we can't service you anymore."
- His conclusion: you become great at sales negotiation by not needing any one deal, not by learning "corny negotiation tactics" or redlining contracts.

chunks.heading: Hiring: build a pipeline and run it like a sales process
chunks.text:
When Dalton debugs a founder's hiring, the biggest issue is usually that there is no pipeline. Too few candidates at every stage means that if a good one appears, the founder has no leverage and no choices.

- Ideal shape: a thousand possible candidates, 50 passed to a first screen, and so on. Then it doesn't matter if one candidate declines or asks for something you can't give.
- He argues founders often think they compete with Google, but the person who takes a job at a company of tens of thousands is probably not the same person who becomes employee number 10 at a startup. The overlap is smaller than people think, so you are usually competing with other early-stage startups, which is easier.
- Pitch the adventure: tell candidates about the responsibility they will have and the hardest challenges (his example is the website going down over the weekend). If a candidate looks at you weirdly, they aren't right. You have more leverage than you think with people excited by that, and far less with someone who wants a pre-IPO spot at OpenAI with the least work for the most money.
- If hiring is a big issue post-PMF, put as much effort into it as into sales. He says the emotional energy needed is on par with getting customers, because you are selling a job at your company. All the same advice about sales applies, and "I put up a job listing, why is no one applying" is not a process.
- Winning is the pre-work, not ninja tricks at the end of negotiation.

chunks.heading: Marketing and PR: tell your own story
chunks.text:
Dalton says founders over-index on getting press (his examples: The New York Times, TechCrunch), thinking "if I can get TechCrunch to write about me, I made it."

- At YC they tracked how many clicks, signups or customers founders got from press, and the result was shockingly small in directly measurable terms. Press is nice because your parents see it, but founders were disappointed when they looked at their dashboards.
- Needing someone else to tell your story is low leverage. High leverage is telling your own story by posting constantly, over and over, with no gatekeepers.
- His test for content: would you want to consume it yourself? The same goes for outbound email: would you respond to it, or want to kill the company that sent it?
- He calls press the anti-best-practice for the last five to ten years. This video series exists for that reason: they didn't think their stories would be expressed adequately unless they got on camera themselves, rather than being guests on someone else's show, possibly for a "fake controversy."
- It takes time but creates value. The same muscles apply to fundraising and recruiting, and a direct channel lets potential users know you are the person who will help them.

chunks.heading: Closing principle: win through pre-work
chunks.text:
Dalton's summary is that winning is about how much leverage you have, not how much people will give you. Founders can feel they have little leverage, but there is often a lot they can do, especially against other startups.

- It is "usually the pre-work", not the final negotiation. By the time you arrive at the negotiation, you have already won.
- Analogy: Usain Bolt's 10-second race involves more than zero work, but it is the years of work beforehand that matter.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton and Michael argue most startups die of suicide, not homicide, and that quitting guarantees failure. Failing early is the natural state, success usually takes longer than founders think, and you should quit only once your hypothesis is clearly answered or for money or health reasons.

chunks.heading: Why most startups die from giving up, not from competitors
chunks.text:
- Dalton says most startups die of suicide rather than homicide: running out of hope is what makes founders quit.
- His logic: if you give up, there is a 100% chance you will not succeed.
- He says the natural state of startups is that they are failing.
- He warns of a "dysmorphia" where everyone else's startup seems to be going better than yours. It isn't.
- If it doesn't feel like it's working, you are probably right, and that is what you should expect.
- Part of his aim in this talk is to help founders feel fired up, and to back that up with logic rather than just adding fuel.

chunks.heading: Successful companies usually took longer than founders think
chunks.text:
- Founders get in their heads that successful companies succeed quickly, because their examples come from Twitter or TechCrunch.
- Dalton suggests using AI to get the real facts. List 10 companies you like, or the 10 apps on your phone, and ask how long each took to do the thing it is known for.
- He says some will have taken years to figure out their business.
- What he tries to comfort founders with: there are many roads to success, and most are longer than you think.
- If it's year one and you are not Cursor yet, you don't have enough evidence to know whether it will work.

chunks.heading: Don't repeat year one over and over
chunks.text:
- A common failure Dalton sees: founders repeat year one repeatedly. They pivot or start something new, but never get past year one and never actually learn something or build a good product.
- Quitting or switching because it isn't working quickly enough means you never reach the point of knowing.
- Legitimate reasons to stop: you are literally out of money, or your health is suffering.
- If the reason is "why aren't we taking over the world yet?" or embarrassment that expectations aren't met, he says to reframe your thinking.
- He says to give yourself enough surface area to be lucky.

chunks.heading: Be careful with the voice in your head
chunks.text:
- Don't be your own worst critic. Negative self-talk about your startup is self-defeating.
- He frames giving up early as validating the bad kind of authority figures: "Don't you want to stick it to the man?"
- He notes that this period is so common it has a name, the "trough of sorrow". Being named means almost everyone goes through it, which is a sign you are not alone.
- Founders usually only admit how bad it was after they succeed. Investors don't advertise their bad investments either, so you rarely hear it.

chunks.heading: What the bad stretch looks like, and why advice won't fix it
chunks.text:
- Dalton describes the typical state: you work hard but aren't sure what to build, and ideas shift every week ("what if we added agents?", "let's put in an MCP").
- You read tweets and tech press about everyone else doing better, which makes you want to pivot to copy what's working.
- You are probably not talking to your users.
- People in this state want authority figures to make them feel better.
- In office hours, founders would ask, "Dalton, what should we pivot to?" and he would answer, "I don't know, man."
- His advice: learn to enjoy the process, realize it's normal, and dig deep. The answer comes from talking to users and shipping product, not from getting into a bad mental state.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton Caldwell's 2012 open letter recounts Facebook executives pitching an acqui-hire to neutralize his competing app, and uses it to argue that ad-funded platforms turn on their developers. He lays out platform risk and his thesis that future social platforms should act like infrastructure with clear business models.

chunks.heading: Platform risk and the Facebook M&A "formula" (June 13, 2012 meeting)
chunks.text:
- Dalton was building an iOS app and service on the Facebook Platform and Open Graph. Facebook developer-relations staff had reassured him it was an interesting, valuable use of the platform.
- He went into a meeting at Facebook HQ (Menlo Park, 4:30 p.m., June 13, 2012) hoping for executive-level support for his launch. Present were a VP Engineering & Products, a VP Partnerships, a VP Corporate & Business Development, and the Director of Developer Relations/Open Graph.
- Facebook's executives told him his product competed with their newly announced App Center. They said they would hate to compete with his "interesting product" and wanted to acquire his company to help build App Center.
- He refused an acqui-hire. He said he would only entertain a serious conversation about acquiring his team and product, and that otherwise he would "rather reboot my company" than see the product shut down and join Facebook.
- The platform executive did not defend his position. He explained that new ad units gave him responsibility for over $1B/year in ad revenue, and that Dalton's product's success would be an impediment to those revenue goals. Offering an acquisition was framed as a kind gesture.
- Dalton's lesson: building on an "open platform" owned by a company with conflicting ad-revenue goals carries huge platform risk. He concluded he got what he deserved for taking "this foolhardy risk."

chunks.heading: Intimidation as negotiation
chunks.text:
- Dalton says other startup founders and Facebook employees told him his experience was not isolated and was part of a systematic M&A "formula."
- He distinguishes being "good negotiators" from implying you will destroy someone's business built on your "open platform." He says these are "not the same thing."
- He draws on years of experience with intimidation-based negotiation tactics from dealing with the music industry (his imeem experience), and calls bad-faith negotiations "inexcusable."
- After the meeting he gave direct feedback about how unhappy he was to one of Facebook's executives, who apologized and said he would take it under consideration.

chunks.heading: Why he vowed to stop building on ad-supported platforms
chunks.text:
- He resolved "to never write another line of code" for ad-supported "platforms" like Facebook or Twitter. He says he had taken the Facebook risk because the Twitter platform was "even more of a joke."
- His motivation: he wants to build quality social software that does not force users to re-create their friends list or avoid OAuth, and that required enduring platform risk on someone else's network.
- He does not think the people at Facebook or Twitter are bad. He argues employees watching a falling stock price "freak out," and that both companies have shown they will mess with users and third-party developer ecosystems in the name of ad revenue.
- His prediction: once a company starts down the slippery slope of messing with developers and users, he has no confidence it will stop.

chunks.heading: Misaligned incentives between platforms, users and developers
chunks.text:
- He argues Facebook built a business whose financial motivations are not in line with users and developers.
- Facebook once called itself a "social utility." Dalton notes the company had stopped using that term, and implies the reason is the conflict between that promise and its ad-driven model.
- He ends by saying the public markets and employees may give Facebook time to fix the "obvious structural flaws" in its platform business, but that those flaws are structural.

chunks.heading: What he thinks replaces them: platforms as infrastructure
chunks.text:
- He believes future social platforms will behave more like infrastructure and less like media companies.
- He expects a number of smaller, interoperable social platforms with clear, sustainable business models to usurp Facebook and Twitter. These companies would be valued at "a small fraction" of what Facebook and Twitter are, and he is fine with that.
- His principle: "Platforms are judged by the value generated by their ecosystem, not by the value the platforms directly capture."
- He says the change will happen even if his own project (App.net, the paid, ad-free alternative he was launching) is not the mechanism that triggers it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Dalton Caldwell argues Twitter's fork between becoming a realtime API platform and building an AdWords-style ad business was a strategic mistake. Choosing ads forced Twitter to own all screen real-estate, kill third-party clients and lock down data, shrinking its potential versus an ecosystem play.

chunks.heading: Twitter's fork: API platform vs. ad business
chunks.text:
Dalton remembers early Twitter as having almost no traffic, with a global firehose on the front page that was "mostly employees and their friends talking to each other."
